The nature of jets in nearby galaxies emitting gamma-rays remains unclear. It's proposed that a specific jet component, associated with molecular disks formed when stars and interstellar material are consumed by a supermassive black hole, could explain the missing power in these systems. However, determining the contribution of these disks and identifying them in the data has proven to be challenging. We introduce two indicators specifically designed to detect these disks and estimate their mass, both related to the total luminosity of the disk and the accretion rate at its inner edge. By applying these indicators to a sample of 21 nearby galaxies with extensive data, we found that their disks all have similar characteristics and are capable of illuminating their surroundings and shining in the gamma-ray range. It's also observed that the distribution of gamma-ray and optical luminosity suggests that the dominant emission component shifts from optical to gamma-rays as the disk mass decreases. Moreover, a correlation between the black hole's spin and the average density of these systems, including their electron density, reveals that the power generated in these systems is influenced by their magnetic properties rather than their mass. It's further proposed that the gamma-ray and optical components in these systems have different origins, with the optical emission resulting from the formation of magnetic fields in the disks and the gamma-rays from the magnetic fields themselves as they interact with the surrounding low-density plasma. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose. However, accurate identification of heart sounds from poor-quality recordings, often obtained in real-world settings, presents a significant challenge. In this study, a novel approach is introduced to categorize heart sounds with minimal reference recordings, incorporating two key features. Firstly, the model can differentiate between clean and noisy training data, and secondly, it can distinguish between sounds even if they are significantly deformed due to external noise. The introduced method comprises two stages where the first stage involves a deep neural network that compares the sounds based on their clean and noisy versions, and the second stage uses a U-Net to compare the sounds based on their spectral features. The model was tested on the PhysioNet Heart Sound Classification Challenge and the results show that it outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the model was able to correctly classify 77% of the deformable heart sounds from only three reference recordings. The introduced method demonstrates significant potential for real-world applications where recordings are often obtained in noisy environments. The model has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghasemian/HeartSoundCategorization. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like fitness trackers and smart wristbands allows users to easily access health data, leading to an explosion of consumer-based health data. Unfortunately, machine-based health classification models trained on cloud-based data struggle to accurately predict outcomes from user-contributed data due to privacy concerns. This causes valuable health knowledge to be locked within the data, inaccessible to the broader medical community. In response, we've developed a novel, lightweight framework called FedHealth, capable of seamlessly integrating user-based health data into a secure, cloud-based environment while discovering meaningful, generalizable insights. This breakthrough enables medical professionals to leverage collective knowledge from various individual cases, enhancing overall classification accuracy and paving the way for more widespread, secure medical knowledge sharing. For large-scale software projects, having an automated build process in place is now considered standard practice. However, as projects evolve, the complexity of their build processes often grows, leading to cumbersome manual configuration efforts. In response, various automated build tools have emerged, streamlining the build process by requiring minimal input. Despite these advancements, build processes continue to expand in complexity, necessitating more sophisticated automated solutions. This thesis introduces a novel approach, building on top of existing automated build systems, that employs machine learning techniques to discover hidden dependencies and optimize build configurations for better performance. By refining existing automated build processes, this approach can rectify issues with outdated dependencies, eliminate unnecessary modules, and even uncover hidden module relationships. In addition, it develops a personalized recommendation strategy for efficient build configurations based on specific project requirements. This thesis further explores the application of its methodology to adjacent problems, such as streamlined software installation processes. In summary, this research focuses on refining automated build processes in software development projects. It achieves this by integrating machine learning with automated build systems, thereby uncovering concealed dependencies, reducing redundant modules, and revealing hidden intermodule connections. It also develops a personalized recommendation method for optimal build configurations and extends its methodology to related problems in the past research. It has successfully been put into practice on real-world projects, demonstrating its practical efficacy. It is now positioned to benefit the broader software development community by providing a platform for (1) automated build configuration guidance, (2) outdated library detection, (3) redundant module removal, (3) hidden module dependency discovery, (4) efficient build configuration recommendations, (5) intelligent installation processes, and (6) various other uses listed in chapter 5. It does this through available source code on github at https://github.com/aminrahmd/SDTool. Our analysis highlights the LHC's capacity to distinguish between certain Scalar Leptoquark combinations using existing energy levels. Specifically, we demonstrate how the LHC can differentiate between certain Pair-Production modes of Second-Generation Leptoquarks, namely Lakshas (LQ) paired with their charge-conjugate counterparts. Our study evaluates the sensitivity of the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the 13-TeV LHC benchmark. For the pair production of Singlet Leptoquarks, we find that the 100 GeV LHC can achieve 3σ sensitivity with as little as 30 fb^-1 of data. Conversely, the 13-TeV LHC requires at least 137 fb^-1 of data to confidently detect the 400 GeV Doublet Leptoquark pair. Additionally, we found that the 13-TeV LHC can distinguish between the 400 GeV Singlet and Doublet Leptoquark pairs with as little as 5 fb^-1 of data. If a Singlet Leptoquark is discovered at the 13-TeV LHC, we recommend searching for the Doublet Leptoquark pair via Drell-Yan production to better understand the Leptoquark sector. Our research originally appeared in the "Phenomenology of Leptoquark Particles" arXiv paper.

The rapid spread of the COVID-19 epidemic has underscored the significance of mathematical modeling in informing public health policy. This paper provides an overview of prominent modeling frameworks used to analyze epidemiological data, focusing on basic reproduction numbers and compartmental models that incorporate different infection periods. We examine the underlying assumptions of these models, including their ability to account for variable infection durations and their impact on epidemiological parameters. Additionally, we discuss approaches to estimating the distribution of infection periods and modeling strategies, such as the application of renewal equations and the use of next-generation matrices to analyze model stability. With an emphasis on clear exposition, this review aims to supply early-career researchers and graduate students in the fields of mathematics and epidemiology with a comprehensive understanding of these methodologies. Furthermore, this review is intended for professionals in these fields who are seeking a refresher on these concepts. With the ongoing significance of modeling in responding to the COVID-19 epidemic, this review is poised to be a valuable resource for some time to come.

As the quantity of data on the internet grows exponentially, there is an increasing need to develop efficient and scalable storage systems that can handle hierarchical structured data effectively. Moreover, with ongoing advancements in cloud computing and distributed storage technologies, there is a rising interest in self-sustaining storage systems that can operate independently with minimal maintenance requirements. In the context of self-sustaining storage systems, it's essential to have a reliable and efficient method for updating stored information with minimal disruption. This research introduces a self-sustaining DNA storage technology capable of efficiently storing hierarchical data and updating stored information with high precision. It outperforms existing DNA storage approaches in terms of data encoding efficiency, information update accuracy, and the frequency of required maintenance. Specifically, it can encode data at a rate 2.44 times faster and requires 35.7% less frequent maintenance than the current record-holder. Moreover, it excels in data encoding efficiency and the ease of information update, making it a more practical solution for real-world applications. This technology has the potential to be used in a wide range of self-sustaining storage systems, finite resources storage, and hierarchical data storage platforms. This research also demonstrates a proof-of-concept for a self-sustaining DNA storage system capable of operating for an indefinite period with minimal maintenance, coupled with an accessible online platform for managing and updating information within this system. This storage system has the capacity to store approximately 1.8 terabytes of data and can update this data with high precision using a simple, efficient method. This research opens the door for further exploration into self-sustaining storage systems, coupled with an accessible online platform for managing and updating information within these systems, and provides a foundation for developing more advanced and complex self-sustaining storage systems in the future. Our proposed method employs a deep neural network (DNN) to bypass the need to directly numerically resolve the shallow water equations in specific situations, where the equations describe combined flows of water waves and tidal currents, particularly in the inner regions of the North Sea. By integrating a fast numerical solver for the shallow water equations, our technique solves the nonlinear equations rapidly, while the DNN efficiently resolves the linear part of the system quickly. Together, they provide a highly efficient hybrid solver that outperforms both the standalone fast numerical solver and the full nonlinear solver from the CHAmbre open-source hydrodynamic model for solving the Helmholtz equation in this context. However, our DNN model can be applied more broadly, not limited to the North Sea. It delivers superior performance when compared to popular state-of-the-art deep learning hydrodynamic models, notably surpassing their speed and accuracy in many cases. Additionally, our model exhibits robustness when dealing with varying water depth, as demonstrated by its successful application to both the global and local scenarios. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/DeepH2O/shallow-water-DNN. Moreover, pre-trained DNN models are available for download at https://deeph2o.org/shallow-water-DNN.

The results presented can be applied to a broad category of random permeability scenarios, and have implications for the development of mathematical models that accurately predict the behavior of complex geological systems. We have developed a comprehensive model to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between an arbitrary number of optical waveguides or resonators, arranged in any configuration. This general approach overcomes the limitations of previous individual mode and coupled mode analysis by allowing for a unified treatment of linear interactions, as well as Kerr nonlinear cross-talk or coupled effects between multiple waveguides or resonators. This has been demonstrated as an equally applicable model for both two-dimensional waveguides and one-dimensional chain of resonators. By utilizing a transfer matrix approach, we derived the matrix that describes both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the waveguides or resonators. This matrix can be used to solve various problems, including mode sorting, beam splitters, and optical buffers, and provides a straightforward method for calculating both linear and nonlinear mode structure, as well as the phase and amplitude of forward-propagating light. This model has been specifically applied to a chain of micro-ring resonators, revealing that it can act as a multi-channel beam splitter, capable of efficiently sorting different optical modes, in addition to demonstrating phase and amplitude stability in a buffer configuration. This general model is suitable for a broad range of optical components and arrangements, and can be easily extended to include additional interactions by modifying the transfer matrix. Furthermore, this approach provides valuable insights into the fundamental differences between linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions, as well as offering practical guidance for designing and optimizing optical components and arrangements. This model has been made available online as a resource for researchers to build upon.

Creating intelligent agents that can excel in dynamic, unknown environments for an indefinite period poses a significant challenge. This problem is particularly difficult because typical evaluation frameworks, designed to assess agents within time-limited settings, aren't effective for assessing the performance of agents in perpetual environments. To address this issue, we present a novel platform called L2Explorer, an endless online multiplayer game of exploration and platform management. This platform allows our evaluation methodology, which incorporates continuous assessment through controlled co-evolutionary processes, to be demonstrated. Over time, successful agents adapt to the dynamic nature of the game by learning essential skills such as platform management and effective exploration strategies. The platform includes multiple evaluation metrics that reflect real-world performance, including the speed at which new locations are discovered and the efficiency of platform management. Furthermore, L2Explorer is open-source, enabling researchers to customize the game world and develop their own evaluation protocols. The platform comprises 11 pre-existing simple agents and 5 complex challenges, each represented by a distinct game world. Above this mass threshold, the ratio of star formation to stellar mass begins to decline in more massive galaxies. We contend that the emergence of this inverse proportionality in more massive galaxies can be attributed to the development of bulges. We selected a subgroup of galaxies with established bulge-dominated properties and compared their SFRs to those without such characteristics at the same stellar mass range. The absence of a turning point in the SFR-to-mass ratio is observed within the bulge-dominated galaxy population, indicating that the ratio instead follows a linear decrease with mass. Consequently, when considering bulge and disk components separately, their respective SFR-to-mass ratios exhibit linear behavior over the analyzed range, without any deviation from linearity observed in the combined galaxy data. The linear dynamics applicable to the individual components provide valuable insights into the local physics governing the M*-SFR relation. The proportionality constant for bulge SFRs, however, reveals a distinction from the constants observed in disk SFRs and the overall galaxy population, further influenced by environmental context. The surge of large-scale image datasets contaminated with inaccurate annotations in tasks like object detection and image classification has negatively impacted the performance of these systems when applying them to unrelated tasks. For instance, a model pre-trained on a flawed cooking image database may incorrectly label a fire as a cooking ingredient. Currently, common practices like using clean datasets for training and evaluating the model's robustness with robustness metrics fail to address these difficulties. A novel approach is proposed that takes into account the presence of erroneous positive associations and introduces a method that takes the precision of the data into account when selecting features for modeling. This approach can be incorporated into models through an additional precision-aware loss function, providing a precise estimate of the precision of the associations detected. Experimental results demonstrate the precision-aware model's superiority over conventional methods in various tasks. We've performed an in-depth analysis of 19 galaxy clusters at high redshift (z= 2.4-3.0) within the ULTRA-DEEP LEGACy fields, focusing on galaxies with minimal starburst activity and moderate to high masses. We found that unlike galaxy pairs at lower redshifts, paired galaxies in this high-redshift cluster sample aren't typically engaged in intense starburst activity or black hole accretion. Instead, they primarily exhibit balanced mass growth, with some slight bulge formation. However, we did identify a subset of galaxies with irregular structures, lacking massive starbursts or active black holes, and characterized by directed accretion and outside major mergers. These external mergers led to directed gas accretion, specifically towards the outer galactic regions, contributing to bulge construction and disk flattening. Despite this, we note that most galaxies within the cluster are uneven and calm, with little bulge formation and directed accretion only towards the centers, contradicting prior assumptions about constant major mergers at high redshifts. Rather, we propose that most galaxies within the cluster are instead governed by slow, cold gas accretion, with some minor star creation, and that the structure of the disk is instead influenced by the angle of this accretion. The resulting disk structures range from flat with prominent bulges to uneven with minimal bulge formation, supported by low levels of starburst activity and black hole accretion. The absence of paired galaxies engaged in intense starburst or black hole activity also supports this model, allowing the cluster to mature slowly over time. The lack of massive star creation within the clusters also allows for the direct observation of low-level bulge construction outside the central regions, further validating the accretion-based model. The calmed and uneven nature of the galaxies within the cluster may also explain the differing rates of galaxy cluster formation in the early universe. The absence of star formation within the central regions of some galaxies may also be attributed to the presence of massive black holes, but due to the lack of active black hole activity in the cluster, we cannot confirm this theory. The rapid dissemination of news on social media platforms is eclipsasing traditional news sources, but also increases the spread of false information. False news can be destructive, especially in the early stages of a developing event, making it vital to tackle this problem quickly. Prior approaches to counterfeit news detection, even those using deep learning techniques, have significant drawbacks in this context. They suffer from overreliance on well-trained models and struggle to adapt to new, unfamiliar situations with limited data. In response, this research introduces a groundbreaking approach that employs a meta-algorithm to anticipate the structure of counterfeit news distributions based on general knowledge. This anticipated framework serves as the foundation for a flexible counterfeiting classifier that can be easily reconfigured for unfamiliar data with just a few instances. Our system's capacity to adapt to new data with ease, demonstrated through empirical results, showcases its utility in detecting counterfeit news across various domains. Moreover, our findings revealed that, in contrast to static models, our system excels in counterfeiting situations with limited training data. Moreover, our analysis highlighted the distinct ways that image and text features contribute to the counterfeiting task, further underscoring the importance of incorporating both features in this context. With its ability to effectively handle emerging counterfeit situations, our system offers substantial improvements over conventional approaches in certain conditions, as shown through our results on three separate datasets. The designed Golay complementary structures can be employed to construct waveforms that minimize cross-terms and interference. Complex systems, comprising interconnected components, are ubiquitous in nature and society. Understanding these systems requires analyzing their architecture and dynamic processes. However, obtaining comprehensive information about these systems through direct observation or experimental data is often difficult and costly. This research addresses this challenge by introducing a non-parametric approach using Graph Neural Networks that enables the estimation of a system's architecture and dynamic processes from partial observational data. The proposed method distinguishes itself from existing parametric techniques, which rely heavily on historical data to predict future behaviors. Our approach has several advantages, including reduced reliance on historical data and the ability to handle systems with varying dynamics and unknown architecture. Furthermore, the proposed framework provides actionable insights by identifying controllable components that can be modified to influence desired outcomes. This technique's efficacy is demonstrated through applications to a simple electrical circuit and a real-world supply chain network. The code for this research is available online.

We introduce a novel neural network named Attribute Contrast Network (ACN) that tackles the attribute extraction challenge using contrastive learning. ACN simultaneously handles two contrasting objectives to obtain a well-rounded representation, one that distinguishes positive samples from each other and another that differentiates attributes from each other. We establish a relationship between attribute extraction and ACN's structure, demonstrating that a specific attribute-related layer is essential for effectively learning attributes. With a focus on both instance and attribute contrast, ACN outperforms competing methods on datasets involving single and multi-attribute classification. Our experimental findings also demonstrate ACN's capability to scale to complex tasks involving multiple attributes. We make ACN available open-source.

In multi-channel speech processing, having more than one audio signal can significantly improve source separation and speech enhancement performance.
We analyze the optimal combination of two-channel and three-channel data finds that, in many cases, three-channel information yields only a small performance gain over two-channel information.
This discovery justifies the use of two-channel data in speech reconstruction, making it possible to employ a dual-path model with two-channel inputs.
We propose a Dual-Path Convolutional Recurrent Network (DPCRN) that leverages two-channel information in speech reconstruction.
This DPCRN model comprises two separate channels, each with its own recurrent neural network, that process and combine information to generate the final output.
We evaluate the DPCRN model on three datasets and find it outperforms existing methods when using two-channel data and often matches or exceeds the performance of other methods when using three-channel data.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could truly become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it requires a specific unconnected system parameter configuration, directly related to the unconnected system's frequency ratio with the other two systems. This entanglement emergence is further influenced by the unconnected system's initial atom state. As a result, this unconnected system's non-equilibrium steady-state state can either become more or less entangled with the other systems, depending on its initial state. Consequently, controlling the unconnected system's parameters allows for adjustable, even bi-directional, entanglement switching between the unconnected and the other correlated systems. This finding has implications for constructing complex, non-equilibrium, many-Jaynes-Cummings-Model systems with controllable, long-range, many-body, and inter- and intra-systems entanglements. Lastly, this model shares some similarities with actual physical phenomena, such as coupled quantum cavities and Bose-Josephson coupled systems.

representing the public's emotion towards a particular topic as expressed on Twitter.

for modeling temporal data and extracting important features from tweets. Furthermore,
by incorporating a technique called TF-IDF, the model's performance was found to
be specifically well-suited for analyzing short texts like those found on Twitter.

The concept of a scheme being "effective" has a well-defined meaning in algebraic geometry, particularly when dealing with singularities and divisors on higher-dimensional spaces. However, many significant mathematical applications require a more versatile tool - the ability to approximate a scheme's properties based on its behavior within a limited scope. This paper introduces a new concept - "restricted effectiveness" - which allows us to compare a scheme's properties across different scales, and in doing so, decouples its intrinsic characteristics from its relationship to a given divisor. We show that this property enables us to generate local, topological invariants through the use of homotopy techniques. Furthermore, when the scheme in question is defined over a field of characteristic zero, we demonstrate the relationship between its homotopy properties and its topological invariants, effectively decoupling its homotopy invariants from its geometric properties. Researchers are focusing on the intersection of magnetism, optics, and photonic technology to create highly efficient, miniature systems for processing information. This discovery offers a versatile way to manage the magnetic properties of these systems using low-intensity light, without the need for sophisticated optical techniques. If successfully applied, this method could lead to the development of efficient, miniaturized information processing systems. The predicted phenomena also provide an accessible means of investigating the interactions between light, magnetism, and elasticity within these complex systems.

This research provides a comprehensive exploration of the underlying principles and guidelines for designing effective PAC codes, also known as polar CRC codes. In addition to its generality, it provides specific examples tailored to the LTE standard. Evaluating the best action sequence in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) amounts to a combinatorial optimization problem due to the extensive space in which word orders can vary. To tackle this challenge, we draw inspiration from the principle of minimizing the number of moves required to rearrange a set of elements, taking the target action sequence as the optimal solution. We develop a novel approach, targeting a specific action sequence that serves as our ideal solution, and design a policy to follow which approximates this target sequence by making local, lightweight modifications. This policy is trained using Reinforce, a policy-based method, resulting in a focused and efficient action sequence. By matching the optimal solution exactly, we eliminate the need to warm up our policy, and explore ways to further accelerate convergence. Our proposed model, in both the training and inference phases, outperforms existing methods evaluated on standard translation tasks, including WMT14 English to German, WMT16 English to French, and IWSLT15 German to English. Additionally, our model excels when compared to state-of-the-art non-RL methods, demonstrating its versatility when combining with the advantages of supervised pre-training. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/RL-NMT.

We analyzed data from the Solar Wind Electromagnetic Investigation suite on board the Parker Solar Probe and the Ulysses Solar Wind Electrostatic Analyzer to examine the solar wind energy flux within the inner heliosphere. A new parameter, the solar wind energy flux spectrum's peak frequency, was identified and found to change with solar wind speed. Notably, this frequency shift isn't solely speed-dependent, indicating that the dominant power frequency within the solar wind also shifts with solar wind density in a way that parallels the solar wind's plasma frequency shift. This phenomenon is particularly evident near the Sun, where the power frequency and plasma frequency converge to a similar frequency, surpassing 1 Hz, a phenomenon we attribute to the solar wind's deepest origin, the turbulent solar surface. This surface's own frequency, in turn, is believed to give rise to the solar wind's power spectra's inertial slope breakpoint, which we found to be approximately 2.7, a value considered generic across the inner heliosphere. The solar wind energy flux spectrum's shape also remains unchanged, with power distributions conforming to power-law patterns observed in solar wind turbulence. Theoretical modeling incorporating the energy flux spectrum and sologram analysis of solar wind plasma fluctuations' velocity and density components' power spectra, both obtained from the Solar Wind Probes and Ulysses, are consistent with the findings, although they were produced using a simpler model that prioritized ease of computation over realism. The rapid dissemination of deepfake media poses a significant problem for media credibility. To combat this, an effective deepfake detection method with robustness to manipulations is urgently needed. Primarily, research has focused on single-domain deepfake detection, with most models performing well on their native data sets. However, with the rise of multi-domain deepfake images circulating online, traditional single-domain models struggle to generalize to unfamiliar types of manipulations. In response, this study introduces the MD-CSDNetwork, a novel architecture tailored for detecting manipulations across multiple domains. Comprising an ensemble of cascaded self-attention modules, the MD-CSDNetwork seamlessly fuses feature representations across different domain types without the need for explicit domain knowledge. When evaluated on the Moffnet platform using the Moffnet-Dataset, the MD-CSDNetwork achieves a true positive rate of 0.94 at a 10% false positive rate, surpassing the performance of single-domain models including state-of-the-art Moffnet-based architectures. Moreover, the MD-CSDNetwork demonstrates superior real-world generalizability in detecting newly emerging deepfake images. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, have adapted to the digital age due to increased global connectivity and the appeal of rapid wealth. While traditional pyramid schemes rely on a physical network of participants, their modern counterparts utilize social media platforms and decentralized finance (DeFi) technology. A prominent example of a digital pyramid scam is the Forsage project, which circumvented restrictions imposed by various countries' laws by operating through a complex network of smart contracts on the blockchain. By analyzing Forsage's code and the interactions of its participants, this research exposes the deceptive inner workings of the scheme and its rewards system. It also identifies the various roles played by participants, including those at the top of the pyramid, as well as the sources of their income. By breaking down the code and examining the financial transactions associated with Forsage, this study reveals the illicit activities it facilitates, including offering unregistered securities and money transfer services. Furthermore, it highlights the ways in which the project's designers have attempted to disguise its true nature. This analysis serves as a model for uncovering the underlying structure of similar digital pyramid scams. In recent years, point cloud representations have gained significant traction for various tasks like 3D classification, segmentation, and reconstruction. One notable advancement includes transformation-based methods that leverage global rotational transformations to enhance data efficiency and model invariance. However, these benefits come with challenges, specifically, the introduction of extraneous noise during synchronization. This work introduces a novel smoothing method, tailored for point clouds in transformation-based settings, that targets this introduced noise. Our approach, named the Transformation Point Cloud (TPC) method, utilizes a combination of the Laplacian method and a Gaussian process, specifically chosen to address the noise introduced by synchronizing over global rotations. In experiments, TPC demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional Laplacian smoothing methods, with a notable increase in accuracy for tasks like 3D classification and segmentation. When applied to real-world reconstruction tasks, the method showed potential, albeit with room for improvement, likely due to the limited training data used. The code for the TPC method is available at https://github.com/chenwen1534/tpc.

We also find that SparseGAN generates more diverse and coherent text compared to its rival. When scaled up to massive datasets, SparseGAN demonstrates notable improvements in efficiency. We establish a precise weight hierarchy for GL_2 cusp forms in the context of Kummer theory, building on the connection between Hilbert modular forms of level 3 and Kummer theory established by Boxer and Katsurada. Specifically, we demonstrate that the set of available Serre weights for GL_2 forms is composed of all odd weights greater than 1, consistent with the weight hierarchy derived via Kummer theory and thereby confirming a conjecture previously proposed by Venkatesh. Furthermore, this approach provides explicit lower bounds for the set of attainable Serre weights for GL_2 forms, exceeding the predictive capabilities of Kummer theory. Additionally, we derive analogous conclusions for forms of higher rank, utilizing the geometric construction of Galois representations originally developed by Taylor and Wiles. The methodology employed also entails the derivation of bounds for the minimal Attaching weight at a given prime, as well as the derivation of weight hierarchies for certain families of Diophantine equations, including the general form of Fermat equations and the biquadratic reciprocity law, both in the context of characteristic 0 number fields. The paper at large builds upon the framework introduced in Boxer-Katsurada (Adv. Math. 2021), combining it with the results derived in Bump-Guo (Ann. Math. 2021) to arrive at the weight hierarchies. We establish the precision of a conjectured regularity aspect for hypersurfaces that minimize their total surface energy subject to constraints on their mean curvature and external boundaries, specifically within the framework of a broad class of measures that can serve as a substitute for the concept of having a small number of individual boundaries. This optimization problem is known to model various physical phenomena, including the behavior of liquid droplets in polymeric networks. By developing the concept of isoperimetric remnants, we build on the existing knowledge of minimal surfaces and directly address the issue at hand by applying the recently introduced notion of local Hausdorff closeness. This enables us to demonstrate that minimizing surfaces that have a large amount of measures as boundaries still possess a high level of smoothness. The precise level of smoothness can be determined by calculating the square root of the total measure of these boundaries. The notion that complex elements within a system hinder its overall astuteness has been a longstanding intuition rooted in historical observations. This concept has been reflected in simple yet effective designs, as seen in Henry Petroski's "Evolution's Edge" series. Nevertheless, a rigorous examination of this principle is necessary to ensure it holds substance beyond being a product of biased perception. Utilizing a computational approach and a broad spectrum of examples, this research seeks to explore the relationship between component complexity and the resulting system's astuteness. A measurable standard of astuteness can be applied to systems comprising elements with varying degrees of complexity. A notable finding indicates that the most intelligent systems often incorporate the most sophisticated components, provided those components are well-suited to their specific environment. Conversely, forcing simplicity onto elements within a system that is well-suited to greater complexity may hinder its potential for high intelligence. Ultimately, this research highlights the importance of context in evaluating the relationship between elemental complexity and a system's overall astuteness. It also paves the way for further exploration into a more precise, quantifiable understanding of this interconnection. A related issue worth investigating arises from considering a system's capacity for self-improvement, which could be influenced by its components' individual capacities for self-improvement. Systems comprising the most advanced components may be more prone to being surpassed by those components' future evolution, potentially leaving them in a state of inferiority. This problem is exemplified in the historical example of Microsoft Windows versus Linux. Despite Linux's initially more rudimentary nature, its open-source and malleable design allowed it to evolve and surpass Windows in certain aspects. In contrast, Windows's more sophisticated initial state made it less adaptable to change and thus more difficult to improve. This phenomenon is relevant to the broader context of the relationship between elemental complexity and a system's intelligence, as it suggests a third factor is at play: a system's capacity for self-improvement, which could be a more fundamental determinant of its ultimate intelligence. Systems are often defined by their capacity to maintain and improve themselves, which in turn is influenced by the inherent capacity for self-improvement exhibited by their individual components. This self-improvement can be driven by evolution, programming, or other mechanisms. Systems comprising components with a strong self-improvement drive will inevitably surpass those made up of more rigid, less adaptive components. This work introduces a novel tensor representation, based on geometric measures, to accurately capture the intricacies of a high-dimensional Euclidean space. Unlike the commonly employed vector representations, this approach utilizes pairwise distance information between points, effectively bypassing the need for a coordinate system. We demonstrate how this tensor model can be applied to achieve significant performance improvements in tasks such as neighbor prediction and data classification, by effectively capturing the subtle distinctions between points in a high-dimensional environment. Additionally, we identify a relationship between our tensor model and the existing coordinate-based approach, providing a theoretical foundation for understanding their interconnectedness. Furthermore, we propose a practical algorithm for implementing the tensor model, accompanied by a comprehensive set of experimental results showcasing its efficacy across various real-world datasets. This research paves the way for a broader understanding of the tensor model and its potential applications in other domains. This work is relevant to but not limited to the fields of machince learning, computer science and mathematics. This study is also a response to the recommendations made by Section 3 of the 2020 NIPS conference talk titled "Talk slides: The emerging theory of DeepLearning" given by Yann LeCun. This talk suggested investigating the theoretical foundations of deep learning through a more intuitive geometric learning theory. This study from our perspective started before the mentioned conference talk took place. Building upon the Toda conformal quantum field theory framework introduced in arXiv:2106.03870, this paper establishes the Ward identities of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda CFT using the OPE formalism and Weyl group symmetry. The Toda CFT is reinterpreted in terms of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Weyl group, with the energy-momentum tensor seen as a descendant of the highest weight state. Key identities, the Kac-Wakimoto differential equation and the Toda algebra equation, emerge from the combinatorial analysis of Weyl group relations. A conformal field theory equivalent to the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda CFT is also constructed, demonstrating that the Toda CFT is rational and leading to the classification of the theory's excitations. This in turn maps the Toda CFT mapping to the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Liouville CFT, providing a new perspective on its symmetries and revealing that the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Liouville CFT contains the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Kazakov-Miller-Sergeev integrable quantum field theory as a subsector. The $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda CFT is further found to encompass the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Heisenberg algebras-based integrable quantum field theories introduced in arXiv:2012.05138 and the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ $\beta\gamma$-ghost CFT. The derived Toda CFT is shown to be equivalent to the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda CFT constructed using the Toda screening charges in arXiv:2106.03870, with the Toda Fock-Rosly algebras emerging from the combinatorial analysis of Weyl group relations. We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures. This study is supported by the proofs presented in the work of Bridson and Reid, demonstrating that certain graph categories encompass buildings and implying biautomaticity for the associated groups. Alternatively, this relationship can be established through the verification of finite test sets for left-automaticity and the determination of a recognizable sequence within the group's generator set. Both of these approaches yield biautomaticity directly. The connection between left-automatic groups and group presentations offered by the recognition theorem for hyperbolic groups in the work of Sela can be utilized as a third means of establishing biautomaticity for Coxeter groups. The biautomatic nature of Coxeter groups results from which the left-invariant metrics on the group's automorphism group are quasi-isometric to the word metric. Additionally, this relationship allows for the comparison of the word metrics on different groups, notably revealing the word metrics on $PSL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ and $BPSL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ to be exponentially equivalent. The research presented in this paper has been previously reported on during talks at the 2018 geometric group theory conference in Edinburgh and the 2019 geometric group theory conference in Bonn. The exponential equivalence between the word metrics on $PSL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ and $BPSL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ was also noted by the anonymous referee. Recently, advanced neural interfaces have provided non-invasive alternatives for deciphering brain signals to determine a paraplegic patient's intentions to walk. These intentions are typically inferred from motor imagination protocols. However, over a decade has now passed since the first successful walking assistance was achieved through the restoration of motor function in paraplegics, and despite this progress, the current method remains dependent on the manual manipulation of electrical stimuli through implanted electrodes, albeit with significant advancements in the precision of these interventions. Consequently, there is an pressing need to address the issue of permanently decoding a patient's ambulatory states and gait rhythms without relying on such manual interventions. In our study, we utilized electrocorticogram signals derived from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill to determine their ambulatory states and gait rhythms. Specifically, we identified distinct patterns in the theta-band signal associated with each state and frequency oscillations associated with the different step cycles. These findings provide a groundwork for the development of a state and gait rhythm decoding system based solely on the analysis of these brain signals, eliminating the need for manual interventions. Ultimately, such a system would enable the direct, permanent decoding of a paraplegic patient's intentions to walk.

Beard and Reeves identified a significant class of subgroup distinguishing properties within right-angled Artin groups based on graph properties. Our research reveals that only two categories of division properties can be applied to subgroups of right-angled Artin groups, specifically those with a specific characteristic in relation to their defining graph and those that distinguish finite subsets within the group generated by a particular subset of its elements. Furthermore, we establish that these two dividing properties are equivalent, and in turn, both are tantamount to the property of being a free group. Additionally, our findings include the novel observation that the property of being a free group can be realized within the context of right-angled Artin groups. The connections between these properties also enable us to characterize the subgroups of right-angled Artin groups that exhibit a distinguishing property in relation to their finite subsets and, in turn, this enables us to characterize the subgroups of right-angled Artin groups that are inherently free. The research presented here also yields the conclusion that there exist subgroups of right-angled Artin groups that are not inherently free. The discussed division properties can be found to extend to the context of groups generated by multiple generating sets, thereby providing an expansive class of group distinguishing properties based on graph properties. The research presented here also includes the discovery of a subgroup of $BA_3$ that is not inherently free, thereby offering an alternative proof to a previously unconfirmed statement of the group theory community. Our proposed method, DC-CONNECT, achieves superior performance in predicting nonlinear connections between time series data without assuming structural relationships. DC-CONNECT leverages long short-term memory connectors, effectively using only a fraction of the historical data for better results. In comparison to conventional correlation and Granger causality-based methods, DC-CONNECT demonstrates enhanced accuracy in predicting dynamic connections. Our model excels particularly in identifying absent connections, offering valuable information for designing more efficient vector autoregressive models. Moreover, DC-CONNECT's efficiency enables it to handle large-scale time series data sets comprising hundreds of variables. Our model's performance is showcased across multiple real-world datasets, including finance, electricity, and temperature data. Additionally, DC-CONNECT's connectivity estimates are utilized to eliminate unnecessary variables from a VAR model, demonstrating its applicability in model compression. With the availability of a pre-trained model, DC-CONNECT offers user-friendly connectivity prediction functionality via a web application. The code for DC-CONNECT is openly accessible on GitHub. In a real-world scenario, we successfully applied DC-CONNECT to reduce the variables in a VAR model used for forecasting COVID-19 cases. The code for the related web application and the pre-trained model on GitHub can be found at https://github.com/salesforce DC-CONNECT. The web application is available at https://dc-connect.app. The dataset used for COVID-19 prediction can be found at https://github.com/nytimes/covid-19-data. A cell's movement within a developing embryo is indicative of its biological function, and by analyzing this movement, we can determine the cell's purpose. This paper focuses on using video analysis to identify moving cells in a developing embryo and uses this information to infer the cells' roles. We believe that stationary cells, which remain in one place, are likely precursor cells, whereas moving cells, which change position, are likely tissue-forming cells. We tested this hypothesis on a type of developing embryo called a neuroblast, which consists of a mass of cells surrounding a central brain. Our results show that cells moving towards the brain are more likely to give rise to it than cells that remain in the peripheral cell mass. This research provides a starting point for using computational methods to study cell dynamics and determine the relationship between cell movement and its associated biological function. We intend to expand on this work by integrating cell movement with genetic data to create a more comprehensive understanding of how cells interact with their surroundings to form a brain. We also propose a new metric called the "displacement vector" which describes the direction and speed at which cells move within the embryo. We used this metric to create a model predicting the brain's origin and validating it with actual brain structures serves as proof of concept. Here, we investigate the behavior of a one-dimensional topological system with binary random disorders and find that it surprisingly develops a unique property - the ability to conduct electricity in a specific direction due to its intrinsic topological nature. This property is stable and occurs across various levels of disorder intensity. We identify the topological regime by developing an analytical disorder-averaging method, which reveals that the conductance is influenced by a combination of the disorder distribution and the topological regime. Furthermore, we observe that sharp peaks can form in the conductance distribution, and these peaks arise at the edges of the topological regime. Additionally, we discover that the distribution of the conductance peaks exhibits an exponential distribution, which can be derived from a mean-field analysis. This exponential distribution is a hallmark of a non-rigid, spatially inhomogeneous system and cannot be replicated by a rigid, homogeneous system. This property results in the formation of sharp peaks in the conductance distribution at the edges of the topological regime, and it cannot be replicated by a homogeneous system. We introduce a new model called Distributed Situational Linear Bandits (DSLB), which combines elements from situational and linear bandits. In this model, each user has their own situational context and it affects the context in which arms are optimally played. Furthermore, the context of each user is independent of the others. We consider a scenario where users are connected through a network and learn from a central controller. The key challenge here is that the controller does not have access to the individual contexts. We provide algorithms for both centralized and decentralized settings and prove that they yield near-optimal performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the centralized algorithm achieves a cumulative regret of order $d^2\sqrt{T}$ when the arm contexts are fixed and the contextual distribution is unknown, and the decentralized algorithm attains a cumulative regret of order $\sqrt{T}$ when the arm contexts are unknown. Additionally, we present a lower bound for the centralized setting with fixed arm contexts, indicating that the linearly-dependent-on-dimensionality performance gap is inherent. Lastly, we offer a bandit version of the DSLB model where the context of each user is learned without additional dimensionality cost. Lastly, we discuss the connection between the DSLB and situational linear bandits settings. The centralized algorithm for this setting yields a cumulative regret of order $\sqrt{dT}$ when the arm contexts are fixed and the contextual distribution is unknown, and the decentralized algorithm attains a cumulative regret of order $d\sqrt{T}$ when the arm contexts are unknown. The paper also includes numerical experiments to evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithms. The paper further offers a learning algorithm for the bandit version of the DSLB setting without context learning and discusses its properties. The proposed algorithm is also shown to be computationally efficient, with a linear increase in computation time in response to increasing numbers of time steps per collision period. Organizing complex information systems into clear hierarchies is crucial, but determining the most effective hierarchy calculation methods has become a pressing challenge as the scale of these systems grows exponentially. Presently, multi-step compression techniques, which are the foundation for many hierarchical representations, lack computationally efficient approaches to derive them directly from raw data. This paper introduces an innovative technique, "Hierarchies by Min-Max Expansion" (HME), addressing this issue by seamlessly integrating the construction of multiple hierarchies from a single network representation, leveraging the same compression structures that underpin modern hierarchical models. By seamlessly integrating the construction of multiple hierarchies from a single network representation, HME significantly boosts the performance of computationally expensive methods while delivering uniformity across diverse hierarchies. Furthermore, HME's modular design enables easy incorporation into existing hierarchical models, thereby enhancing their capacity to capture complex relationships within information systems. By applying HME to real-world datasets, our findings demonstrate notable improvements in both computational efficiency and the diversity of hierarchies generated, offering a promising blueprint for developers to refine existing hierarchical algorithms in the pursuit of optimal hierarchies in large-scale information systems. The HME model has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghaffari/HME.

The structure of dense stellar matter is intricately linked with the sound speed, a crucial element in determining the stability of neutron stars. Research indicates that dense matter's electric charge must be considered, especially the presence of strange quarks, which could influence the sound speed and, in turn, the properties of neutron stars. Our study focuses on dense matter with strangeness, modelled as strange hadronic matter or quark matter with colour superconductivity, and calculates the sound speed within various models of dense matter. By correlating the sound speed with other physical parameters, we establish a range for its possible values, ultimately utilizing these predictions to constrain the properties of strange stars and neutron stars. Combining our calculations with existing data on pulsar stars, specifically PSR J1614-2230 and PSR J0348+0432, we calculate the mass ranges for strange stars and neutron stars and compare our findings with theoretical mass ranges from other studies. Our analysis highlights the significance of measuring the sound speed in dense matter to gain a deeper understanding of the behaviour in neutron stars and the importance of considering matter's electric charge. Additionally, we stress that the presence of deconfinement phase transitions in neutron stars may lead to quark gluon plasma formation at their surface. Lastly, our research emphasizes the need for more precise measurements of the sound speed and mass of neutron stars to better comprehend their internal composition and possible strangeness.

This research focuses on a class of manifolds with evolving curvature properties, which we term 'Ricci diminutive with constant scalar curvature', and demonstrates the non-evolutionary nature of these manifolds. Additionally, an applicable Liouville theorem is provided, offering a significant expansion of a priori bounds initially established in (Chen-Dan, arXiv:2103.14511). By leveraging this Liouville theorem and applicable maximum principles, we derive key differential equations that describe the evolution of these manifolds and solve the parabolic equation that defines them, ultimately concluding that the only steady state equation is the flat Euclidean space. This in turn enables us to solve a conformally invariant obstacle problem and retrieve a result on the nonexistence of expanding solitons within the $\mathbb{S}^2$ space. Lastly, we discuss the applicability of this Liouville theorem to a broader class of manifolds and propose several open research questions. This research was conducted in collaboration with B. Yuan.

Our proposed network, DEGP-Net, incorporates a unique entrance structure where information from external sources is combined with internal data via a dynamic routing mechanism. This approach differs from conventional methods as it employs a global mean pooling technique instead of max or sum pooling to determine the weighting factors. The network's flexibility to adapt to diverse external data configurations, such as point clouds with varying densities, makes it particularly suitable for real-world applications. Our experiments demonstrate DEGP-Net's performance in tasks involving external data with varying densities, such as 3D object detection from LiDAR data and point cloud classification. The results show DEGP-Net achieves superior outcomes when compared to standard methods using fixed external data configurations. Moreover, its efficiency in processing external data with variable densities is further illustrated. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are influenced by our solar system's position within the Milky Way and its gravitational effects according to general relativity. A key factor affecting this is the post-Newtonian gravitational parameter $\gamma$, with a well-established value except for very precise measurements. Here, we examine the impact of $\gamma$ uncertainty on parallax magnitudes measured by a telescope like Gaia, with a focus on the lowest-latency measurements. Gaia's measurements for close stars are largely unaffected, but a significant impact is seen on the parallax measurements for distant stars, with a maximum deviation of around 0.0005 trochs for a distance of 10 kiloparsecs. This could be compared with the actual parallax of 3.39 microtrochs for a distance of 10 kiloparsecs. Also, we investigate the $\gamma$ effect on the line-of-sight velocity measurements for stars, with a predicted effect on the order of 0.1 percent. This could be a major consideration for future telescopes with high precision velocity measurements. With a predicted value of 5.01, we discuss possible approaches to estimating the $\gamma$ coefficient from astronomical data. This could also provide an estimate for another post-Newtonian parameter, $\delta$, which affects the Earth's mass measurement but has a much greater impact on the measurement of the Sun's mass. With a predicted value of 4.254 for $\delta$, we examine the effect of this on the measurement of the Sun's mass, with a forecast for future telescopes to measure the Sun's mass with a precision of 2 percent. This could be a major breakthrough in solar physics with implications for the study of the sun's evolution, the behavior of the core, and the energy generated, as well as providing more accurate calculations for gravitational precession in the frame-dragging effect and Lense-Thirring effect, with a predicted value of 7.48 arcseconds for the sun's effect on the Gaia telescope. This research underlines the significance of taking general relativistic effects into account when designing high-accuracy astronomical telescopes. This could also provide a simpler approach to estimating the $\gamma$ coefficient from astronomical data with a predicted value of 1.002 for Gaia with Gaia-like telescopes with a longer baseline with a forecast to measure the Sun's mass with a precision of 1 percent. To enhance the semantic understanding of questions in open-domain Commonsense Question Answering, we introduce a novel approach that explores a hybrid search path combining coarse and careful reading strategies. Initially, a rough search identifies relevant knowledge, and a subsequent in-depth analysis refines the understanding of the question with the aim of integrating a more precise semantic connection. We develop a step-wise approach consisting of three phases: an initial coarse reading to generate a question's semantic profile, a careful reading to determine the appropriate knowledge domain, and a fusion phase that combines the results from both readings to produce a comprehensive semantic representation. We further propose a novel Coarse-to-Careful Question Answering Framework (CCQAF) to effectively implement this approach. Comprehensive evaluations on the Commonsense Question Answering Dataset show that our method significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art models, and the individual components of the model also demonstrate strong performance. Moreover, CCQAF achieves superior results when evaluated on the SQuAD v2.0 dataset. The code for CCQAF is available at https://github.com/ghru/CCQAF.

Federated learning allows multiple parties to collaborate on model development while keeping their data privately owned. However, diverse data sets complicates the optimization process, making it difficult to achieve balanced contribution from participating institutions. This issue is particularly problematic in educational settings, where diverse data sets are common and contributing institutions often have different demographic profiles. This paper presents a new, efficient algorithm called stroll for the high-dimensional, sparse data scenario prevalent in educational applications. This efficient method allows for a significant reduction in the computation required for each institution to contribute to the model. Additionally, the stroll algorithm prioritizes institutions with the most valuable contributions, helping to address the problem of diverse data sets. This paper also introduces a new concept, "density gap", to facilitate fair model development in educational applications. Experimentation with real data demonstrates the effectiveness of the stroll algorithm. This algorithm is particularly well-suited for educational applications, where the data sets are often sparse and diverse. This paper also explores the use of the stroll algorithm with noisy data, finding that it can still converge to the optimal solution with a moderate level of noise. This algorithm has been implemented and is available online. This research also provides a solution to the problem of diverse data sets in non-educational settings, as well as an analytical framework for the stroll algorithm with noisy data. This paper presents the results of this research, including the stroll algorithm, the density gap concept, and the analytical framework, which are all applicable to non-educational settings. Research indicates that incarcerated individuals experience poor mental health, with high rates of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, and anxiety. Upon release, this population faces significant barriers to care, exacerbating already disadvantaged social circumstances. For convicted offenders, mental health issues are not necessarily a prerequisite for a sentence related to mental health acts. Judge-ordered therapy, which can result from offenses not directly tied to mental health, may effectively provide access to necessary care, improving an individual's mental health and reducing reoffending. To date, studies examining the effects of therapy ordered by the court have focused primarily on reoffending and mental health benefits, with limited exploration of how such therapy influences psychological well-being (PWW) in this population. Utilizing a retrospective cohort study design, this research assesses the impact of court-ordered therapy on the psychological well-being of incarcerated individuals with sentences related to mental health acts. The findings indicate that, in comparison to similar individuals not ordered to undergo therapy, those who received therapy had greater psychological well-being, with the beneficial effect being more pronounced in the long term. Additionally, the mental health benefits associated with therapy were found to extend to the point of release from prison. Consequently, this research provides evidence to support the inclusion of psychological interventions as part of sentences related to mental health acts, aiming to enhance the psychological well-being of this population and, by extension, their chances of leading law-abiding lives upon release. Key findings also highlight the extended mental health benefits of such interventions during the transition to community life. Given the limited scope of current research, further investigation is warranted to explore the effectiveness of therapy in reducing reoffending in this population. Given its focus on psychological well-being, this research offers a valuable contribution to the existing body of work, with implications for policy and practice within the criminal justice system. Given its retrospective cohort study design, this research controlled for various confounding variables that could influence both the decision to order therapy and the outcome of interest (i.e. psychological well-being), thereby enhancing its validity. To generalize these findings to other populations and settings, this research highlights the need for replication in different contexts. Given the findings related to PWW and the associated methodological discussion, this research offers a valuable resource for researchers seeking to explore this concept in other populations and settings. Given its focus on outcomes rather than processes, this research provides a valuable template for designing and analyzing studies focused on the effectiveness of interventions in other contexts. A pervasive issue in healthcare image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper addresses the challenge of refining image segmentation models with limited annotations. We propose a simple post-processing technique, "Sort and Jitter," which reorders pixels by their probability maps and applies Gaussian noise to create a target distribution. This target distribution is then used to regularize the model through a consistency loss. We test this technique on publicly available datasets and compare it to established methods, demonstrating improved performance with less computational expense. Code is available at: https://github.com/ghru/BasicRegTech.

The behavior of multiple interacting particles under certain conditions can suddenly become wildly unpredictable, which is known as the onset of classical chaos. In statistical mechanics, this phenomenon occurs when three or more objects interact with each other via the same simple connection. Research has shown that this kind of chaos affects individual particles differently, with some experiencing massive, sudden changes and others remaining largely unaffected. To better understand this phenomenon, particularly how it affects individual particles, we propose a new way of analyzing complex interactions using a machine learning technique called graph neural networks. This method allows us to identify how differently each particle behaves and how they respond to changing connections. By using this technique on a simple example, the dynamics of individual particles become visible as unique patterns of behavior on a numerical map. This discovery provides a clear visual understanding of how individual particles behave in complex, chaotic situations. To take it a step further, we found that this pattern of behavior can be calculated using a simple mathematical formula, which gives us a more direct way to analyze the behavior of individual particles. To make this analysis more reliable, we tested it on a randomly generated group of particles and found that it accurately predicted their behavior. To apply this technique to real-world situations, we showed that it can be used to analyze the behavior of particles in an actual laboratory experiment by matching the numerical map with real data. To make it even more useful, we proposed a way to create a similar numerical map for any complex, chaotic system, which could be any number of particles with different types of connections. To validate this proposed map, we tested it on a well-known mathematical equation that generates complex, chaotic patterns when plotted, and found it accurately matched the real data from the same experiment. This research develops an Asymptotic Evaluation Method (AEM) to assess the parameters of a mixture model, extending the Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) method to blends of unknown proportions. The AEM facilitates an analytical understanding of how the mixture parameters are affected by sample characteristics, model characteristics, and sampling design, thereby providing a statistical theory framework for inference in the context of mixture sampling. The study also explores general theory and specific numerical examples of the AEM, demonstrating its utility in predicting the variance of blend parameter estimates and offering insights into the optimal sample size for a given level of estimation precision. Furthermore, the research offers a statistical theory-based solution to the problem of estimating the parameters of a mixture model, specifically the variance of the mixture distribution when only a sample from the mixture is available, with no prior knowledge of the mixing distribution. The findings are illustrated using real data from a study on the composition of a forest ecosystem. The research was conducted in the context of ecological research, but the methods developed are applicable to any blend of unknown proportion. Knowledge tracing, a technology that infers students' knowledge based on their interactions with online educational platforms, has gained significant traction. As knowledge tracing continues to evolve, it has found practical uses in optimizing educational content and personalization for students. Despite these benefits, knowledge tracing models have been found to frequently discriminate against underrepresented minority groups. Furthermore, research has demonstrated that deep learning knowledge tracing models frequently exhibit flawed logic when compared to human subject-matter expertise. In response to these challenges, the default approach of simply training and evaluating knowledge tracing models with accuracy metrics has become inadequate. Instead, researchers now evaluate models through the application of pedagogical theory and various fairness and bias analysis tools. However, prior research has left a significant gap in terms of accessible code for evaluating knowledge tracing models. This paper addresses this shortfall by presenting pyKT, a Python-based framework designed to assist in the fair evaluation of knowledge tracing models through the utilization of standard datasets, efficient data manipulation tools, a diverse range of fairness and bias assessment protocols, and comprehensive logging capabilities. By providing this type of evaluation framework, researchers can concentrate on developing more advanced knowledge tracing models, while simultaneously ensuring these models adhere to high standards of fairness and accurately reflect human subject-matter expertise. The design of pyKT enables easy access to the framework for the broader research community through a straightforward GitHub repository. Words: 250

Constructing precise proof objects for verified decision-making in SAT and SMT solving is crucial for building trust in these systems, especially within applications requiring high-level assurance, such as cryptographic protocols and safety-critical hardware. Currently, the process of creating these proofs is often hindered by inefficient proof generation techniques and the need to cater to diverse format requirements from different verification tools. The rigid input formats demanded by these tools often necessitate a deep understanding of their internal workings, posing a significant obstacle. The proliferation of disparate proof formats contributes to a 'proof format fragmentation' issue, which hampers interoperability and further complicates the verification process. The challenge of validating a widely accepted standard across various verification tools has led to the development of the Alethe proof language, a straightforward and expressive standard that can be seamlessly integrated with existing proof generation techniques. The Alethe standard is compatible with widely adopted formats, including why3's TASTE, and enables efficient proof validation through the use of a highly performant solver, CVC4, which can translate the Alete standard into various verification tools. The development of the Alete standard is ongoing, and is being made available to facilitate discussion and collaboration among the verification community. The associated tools, available at https://alethe.io, comprise a command-line proof validator, a Python API, and a collection of proof translation configurations. The Alete standard, along with the associated tools, has been utilized in our previous work on verifying hardware descriptions, and is currently being employed in the verification of Amazon's Braket quantum application platform. The integration of the Alete standard with other proof formats is also discussed, along with the proof formats used in the Amazon Braket project. As machine learning models are fed into an ever-expanding number of applications, developing safe and effective federated learning algorithms for real-world data is increasingly crucial. A significant limitation of current federated learning techniques hinders its practical use: it typically requires data gradients to be derived under constrained input ranges, checking for boundedness before computing them. Additionally, many modern models, in particular deep neural networks, frequently struggle with these constraints due to the large magnitude of their gradients. In response to these challenges, researchers have explored alternative approaches, such as the use of federated learning with synchronous aggregation, capable of handling gradient constraints and efficiently training large models. Building upon this work, the current study enhances the model by allowing data gradients to be freely generated, incorporating a novel feature called buffered synchronous aggregation. Theoretical analysis along with experimental results confirm the effectiveness of this model in efficiently training high-quality models on diverse datasets with unconstrained data gradients. The model's flexibility and ability to handle large datasets with complex structures make it particularly suitable for real-world machine learning applications. The model's simplicity is further highlighted by the absence of any requirement for clipping gradients, a common practice in many existing models, which can be directly incorporated into the model by simply increasing the buffer size. The model's source code is available at https://github.com/ghru/bsa. The results presented in this study can be reproduced using the same code. The model in question has been successfully applied to train large models on moderately large datasets with unconstrained data gradients in various settings. The model's success in training a model of 1.4 million parameters on a dataset of 200,000 instances has been demonstrated. The model's ability to train models of over a million parameters on moderately large datasets with under 300,000 instances has also been shown. The model's capability to efficiently train deep neural network-based models on various datasets with under 300,000 instances has been proved. The model's success in training a model of over a million parameters on a dataset of 50,000 instances with unconstrained data gradients in 25 hours has been demonstrated.
