Our proposed method leverages a strong English speech recognition model to enhance a limited amount of data for training an Italian speech recognition model. The approach employs a multilingual acoustic model, incorporating the existing English model while maintaining the Italian phonetic characteristics. We employ a style-invariant vector, extracted from a contrastive self-supervised Italian speech pretraining model, to preserve the distinct Italian pronunciation features. The resulting model demonstrates a 9.5% improvement in WER when compared to the baseline system, utilizing a significantly smaller training dataset. Additionally, we achieve comparable results with a more extensive Italian training dataset. Our model also exhibits strong performance when evaluated on a cross-language Italian-English speech recognition task, outperforming a state-of-the-art Italian model by 12.3% in WER. The model's efficacy in preserving national pronunciation characteristics is further illustrated through an experiment conducted on a Scottish English speech recognition dataset, where it achieves a 14.6% WER reduction. Our approach can be applied to other language pairs and we provide comprehensive implementation details. Our code is available at https://github.com/parthk/RF-TD-CLASR.

In marine navigation, obtaining accurate velocity readings is critical, and optical flow is a promising technique with high potential for real-time applications. However, optical flow on the open sea is prone to significant velocity estimation errors due to constant water velocity misleading the algorithm. Additionally, optical flow and other navigation sensors produce different time samples, requiring interpolation to match their trajectories. We introduced previously a Gaussian Process Temporal Variation model to address the sampling discrepancy, and now a new, more efficient model has been developed to handle both discrepancies and predict the true trajectory of the robot. This prediction allows for precise velocity estimation essential for safe robot navigation. We tested the model on synthetic data and real-world recordings of the sea surface and naval movements, and also conducted naval experiments with a Gaussian Process and a kernel-based filter to navigate through narrow courses in the open sea. The results showed that the model effectively learns the temporal variation of the sea surface and accurately predicts the robot's true trajectory even with large water velocities and narrow navigation courses. The challenge of fairly distributing irrevocable goods to self-interested individuals in an environment where manipulation is possible, as identified by an initial observation in the 1980 "College Admissions" problem, has persisted for decades. This issue has been shown to result in an inequitable outcome in an environment with strategic behavior. In an effort to address this long-standing difficulty, we focus on finding a distribution method that produces equilibria in which all participants are satisfied with their assigned good, regardless of whether the distribution is fair. We demonstrate that, with the exception of specific instances, there is generally no distribution algorithm capable of producing a distribution that is fair and also a pure Nash equilibrium. We also examine various specific situations and present an optimized algorithm for addressing the problem of finding a pure Nash equilibrium in an environment where goods can be divided. This optimized algorithm enables us to determine fair and equitable distributions in scenarios where sharing is possible, as well as in the original college admissions problem. In these environments, we find that the student-optimal stable distribution, a distribution that is highly desirable due to its fairness properties, is not resilient to manipulation and is therefore not a pure Nash equilibrium. In contrast, the same algorithm reveals that the following distribution, which we call the efficient competitive equilibrium, is resistant to manipulation and is therefore a pure Nash equilibrium, and it has the additional benefit of maximizing overall satisfaction when sharing is possible. This shows that, in the context of division-based environments, fairness is not necessarily a prerequisite for resilience to manipulation. In fact, we can demonstrate that in an environment where sharing is possible, the most equitable distribution, the one that results in the maximum overall satisfaction, is not unique when considering the behavior of self-interested individuals. In such an environment, the unique distribution that arises from considering the behavior of self-interested individuals is the one that maximizes overall satisfaction when sharing is possible, but it does not have any known explicit expression. This finding highlights that, when sharing is possible, the term "efficient envy-free" is actually a misnomer, as there are multiple distributions that are resistant to manipulation and result in the absence of envy when sharing is possible, as they both maximize overall satisfaction when sharing is possible. In contrast, when sharing is not possible, the unique distribution that results from considering the behavior of self-interested individuals is the one that maximizes overall satisfaction without sharing, and it has the explicit expression of being the largest item first. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning for
these scenarios is challenging due to the diverse nature of available data,
including mixed sets of successful and failed experiences. In particular,
offline learning often struggles with failed experiences, especially those
resulting from individual agent failures rather than poor policy design.
Currently, methods simply discard such data without utilizing its
informative value. This issue becomes even more problematic when data
includes incomplete trajectories, in particular those representing successful
outcomes. This paper addresses these challenges by introducing a new
adversarial training-based approach, capable of learning from diverse
offline data sets that include failed experiences and incomplete trajectories.
By harnessing the information present in these data sets, the approach
extracts distinct positive trajectories and individual agent trajectories
simultaneously. A dual adversarial reinforcement learning mechanism then
enables effective exploration and evaluation of actions across these diverse
trajectories. This approach is validated through experiments conducted on
multiple complex scenarios, including scenarios with individual agent failures
and partially observable environments. The results demonstrate substantial
performance gains achieved by this approach in comparison to existing
methods. The approach is also found to be highly adaptable, as it can be
easily applied to a wide range of real-world problems without requiring
significant adjustments. The code for this approach is available at https://github.com/ghulamabbas/PositiveOfflineMultiAgentLearning.

We developed a novel approach for aligning MV images, utilizing a convolutional neural network, in both 2D and 3D. Utilizing 100 x-ray images and 50 kilovoltage images, we trained two separate networks, one for each image type. Each network consisted of multiple convolutional layers with a U-Net architecture, enabling the direct use of raw images as input. We achieved satisfactory results with both networks, with 2D producing an average alignment error of 3.5mm and 3D producing an average alignment error of 4.3mm. Additionally, we found that using kilovoltage images as a reference resulted in better alignment compared to using electronic portal imaging devices images. Furthermore, we found no significant difference between aligning 2D images from 3D images, and vice versa. Lastly, we found that using our network-trained parameters, we could improve alignment compared to using conventional registration methods. We applied this method to align megavoltage images with kilovoltage images in head and neck cancer patients, achieving an average alignment error of 4.9mm. We believe this method could be useful for calculating dose in kilovoltage images from megavoltage treatments. Additionally, we propose a new method for calculating dose in kilovoltage images from megavoltage treatments, using the aligned megavoltage images. Lastly, we believe this method could be applied to align images from different beam energies.

The notion that entanglement between two particles is necessary for genuine nonlocal effects to occur has been challenging the fundamental principle of locality. Here, we demonstrate that entanglement among individual particles can result in nonlocal effects, potentially even when separated from their respective environments. This nonlocality arises from the interplay between the particles' entanglement and their individual interactions with their environments. This discovery provides a physical explanation for the phenomenon of single-particle nonlocality and underscores the significance of taking into account the particles' individual environments in assessing nonlocal effects. Moreover, it paves the way for exploring the relationship between entanglement, nonlocality, and individual environments in a more comprehensive analysis. Additionally, this finding offers a practical application, with the prediction of a specific nonlocal effect that can be experimentally verified using available technology. Specifically, it can be validated through a series of Bell inequality tests or a scenario in which a particle's trajectory is steered by its entangled partner. This prediction is not only theoretically predicted but also arises from the particle's individual nonlocality, a phenomenon that can be physically experienced as the particle moves through a curved space. This discovery opens the door for exploring the connection between space curvature and nonlocality. Furthermore, by examining the relationship between the particle's entanglement and its individual nonlocality, we can derive a previously unknown, precise criterion for determining the particle's nonlocality based on its reduced density matrix. This research was conducted without referencing its physical basis, making it a purely theoretical analysis that can be applied across different physical contexts. This finding has the potential to be extended to a broader non-equilibrium scenario, thereby providing a general, applicable principle. This principle, known as the "entanglement nonlocality inequality," uniquely connects the particle's internal properties to its external, nonlocal behavior in a curved space. This connection can be expressed through a specific, calculable figure that represents the particle's nonlocality as it moves through space, offering a quantitative understanding of its nonlocal behavior. This research provides a tangible, measurable expression for nonlocality that can be derived from the particle's internal, inherent properties, with the potential to discover new principles governing nonlocal behavior in complex, curved spaces. This discovery also sheds light on the fundamental relationship between space curvature and nonlocality, presenting a calculable figure for nonlocality that can be physically experienced as the particle moves through a curved space, even when its environment is changing over time. The integration of Internet of Vehicles (IoV) technology and education is becoming increasingly essential. IoV education is being shaped by rising tensions between rapid technological advancements and growing security and safety concerns. Blockchain and Federated Learning-based techniques are leading the innovation in IoV education by facilitating secure, private, and efficient learning. Currently, IoV education primarily focuses on developing technologies rather than giving priority to security in areas like vehicle networking and autonomous driving. Consequently, fluke accidents caused by over-reliance on autonomous driving systems and cyber attacks on vehicle control systems due to poor security protocols are on the rise. These issues necessitate the development of secure and trustworthy IoV education frameworks. Presently, IoV education is largely descriptive, lacking concrete data. Nonetheless, research on IoV education is expected to shift towards greater emphasis on security in the near future. This review covers various types of IoV education, including vehicle networking, autonomous driving, and the challenges they pose, as well as the existing literature on IoV education frameworks, especially those powered by blockchain and Federated Learning technologies. Furthermore, it explores the possibilities of Future IoV education, particularly in regards to vehicle networking and autonomous driving, based on historical data and trending analysis. This review also provides an comprehensive overview of IoV education, including its components, the challenges it faces, the existing literature, and its possible trajectory in the near future. This research can serve as a foundation for in-depth examinations of specific IoV education components or future trends in the field. This survey paper on IoV education and its possible trajectory in the near future is suitable for reading by experts in the field as well as newcomers to the subject. This review is also an opportunity to explore various types of IoV education, the challenges they pose, the existing literature on IoV education frameworks, and the possibilities of Future IoV education. In Fast Dialogue Mode (FDM) systems, codebooks are pre-generated to streamline the feedback process, but coding them in advance can lead to inefficiencies. This codebook disparity causes information loss during encoding, resulting in codewords that deviate from optimal reconstruction. To rectify this, we propose a codebook development method rooted in Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs), which minimizes this codeword discrepancy. Furthermore, our scheme complements this approach by enhancing the encoder's performance using codeword post-processing. Both proposed encoders are compatible with FDM codebooks and can be applied across various scenarios, including single-codebook and multi-codebook systems and FDM-Full Dialogue Mode (FDM) transmission. Codebook development and encoder design are both computationally efficient, making our scheme suitable for practical implementations. Numerical evaluations validate the effectiveness of our method, demonstrating reduced codeword discrepancy and improved performance in FDM transmission.

For approximately 10,000 years, the constellation of Scorpius-XN has been observed, revealing that its hydrogen maser flux has remained relatively stable apart from occasional flare-ups and declines in intensity. By examining 20-year data sets from four hydrogen maser sources within Scorpius-XN, researchers found that the maser flux has a specific distribution characteristic, lacking both extremely high or low intensity sources. Using this information and combining it with existing research on Bondi masses in the Chandra Galactic Plane Project, a team was able to calculate the average and total amount of matter being drawn into the supermassive hole at the center of the Milky Way. They found that the average Bondi mass capture rate is extremely low, likely falling below 1 solar mass per year, and the total rate could be as little as 10 solar masses per year, indicating that the pace of mass accumulation at the center of the galaxy is very slow. This finding has implications for the black hole seed population and supports the theory that the growth of the first galaxies was slow. Additionally, it provides a tool for interpreting the distribution of Bondi masses in the centers of galaxies. The team also discovered that the pattern of variability in the maser sources correlates with the brightness of the maser, suggesting that flares are more frequent at lower intensities and flare declines are more common at higher intensities. We examine the possibility that extremely compact binary mergers in the centers of globular clusters, formed from the remnants of the first stars, could be detectable by the LISA gravitational wave observatory. The number of such events is predicted to be quite low, ranging from 0.01 to 100 annually, and would primarily consist of neutron-star–quark-star binaries. The number of these mergers is expected to peak in the 2020s to 2030s at a rate of about one per month, based on theoretical models of the early universe. The total mass of this class of binaries is likely to be tens of thousands of solar masses, placing them within LISA's detection range. The predicted rate of these mergers may also leave a detectable imprint on the gravitational wave background emitted by all binary mergers. In this study, we examine the possibility of enhancing information security in a multi-carrier wireless communication system that employs a dual function amplify-and-forward relay. The system in question meets the criteria for a multi-input multi-output (MIMO) architecture, offering the added benefit of improved end-to-end connectivity. To establish a more secure connection, we suggest implementing a MIMO-based physical layer encryption technique. Following this, we develop and evaluate an optimal power allocation strategy for an improved security solution, along with a comparison to an alternative fair power distribution method. Furthermore, an analysis of the numerical results reveals that the proposed encryption technique delivers superior security performance, while also ensuring satisfactory data transfer rates. Conversely, the fair power allocation method prioritizes faster data transfer rates at the expense of compromised security. The proposed power allocation method is also shown to offer significant advantages over two other schemes, namely single-carrier wireless communication with a dual-function relay and MIMO-based physical layer encryption. The findings of this research are underpinned by numerical data obtained from simulations. The fair power allocation method, on the other hand, delivers the fastest data transfer rates across these same frequency ranges. The proposed power allocation method is also an optimal solution for various other security and data transfer rate scenarios. The study at hand addresses open research questions in the fields of wireless communication and information security. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 moves per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving an astonishing move processing speed of one million moves per second.
By leveraging this incredibly fast processing, we can now conduct extensive tests spanning hundreds of thousands of moves, making the outcome significantly more reliable and indicative of an agent's true capabilities. 
Our findings reveal that the current common assessment method, which only considers the first 20 moves of each test, is indeed flawed and needs revision. 
Our findings also highlight the importance of accounting for the early stages of each test when evaluating an agent's performance. 
TextWorldExpress is available online, awaiting contributions from users who can help further develop this platform by creating new text-based games under an open-source license.

Deep learning networks, particularly LSTM structures, have been highly effective in video recognition tasks but suffer from significant computational requirements and extensive memory needs for large-scale videos. This limitation makes them impractical for real-world deployments on mobile devices. This research addresses this challenge by introducing an energy-efficient LSTM architecture based on Hierarchical Tucker Decomposition (HTD) and employs a novel training method that optimizes both performance and resource utilization. The novel training algorithm employed in this research utilizes a hybrid approach that combines the benefits of both block-wise and layer-wise training methods. This approach is designed to minimize memory consumption during training while preventing performance degradation. Following training, the network is converted into an offline format that can be deployed on resource-constrained devices without the need for additional memory. The results of this research demonstrate the superiority of the HTD-LSTM network over other compressed LSTM structures based on existing methods and its ability to efficiently process large-scale videos with minimal memory needs. The novel training method and energy-efficient HTD-LSTM network developed in this research have the potential for wide-ranging applications in various real-time video recognition scenarios. The code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub at: https://github.com/linglong604/HTD-LSTM. The design of the HTD-LSTM network also enables further customization and retargetting, making it an attractive option for real-world deployments. The Feeble Gravity Conjecture proposes that a hypothetical boundary must include a boundary that is adjacent to a gravitational system in order to possess certain properties. In this paper, we investigate the proposed boundary properties, specifically examining the convexity of the spectrum of a c2-based conformal field theory for charged operators. Our analysis reveals that convexity is not a necessary condition for the spectrum in this context. Furthermore, we establish that the spectrum remains non-convex within the realm of a specific model, thereby refuting the earlier prediction of its convexity. Consequently, the Feeble Gravity Conjecture is substantiated, and it now serves a more significant purpose in understanding the boundary properties of a conformal field theory in one dimension. Additionally, our analysis of the model presents a new means of examining the effects of a nearby gravitational system on a boundary in one dimension. Lastly, this discussion is complemented by an appendix exploring the model within the larger context of semi-classical gravity.

This research paper examines auxiliary services markets in the UK, specifically markets for services that complement electricity and gas retail sales. Our analysis classifies these markets into three categories based on how they interact with the electricity and gas retail markets: those that provide essential background information, those that offer value to specific customer groups, and those with broad applicability. We then review procurement policies for these services, evaluating current approaches and identifying opportunities to develop more tailored strategies that account for the diverse electricity and gas retail markets. Our findings suggest that a more nuanced understanding of auxiliary services and their connections to the electricity and gas retail markets is critical for informing effective procurement policies. Finally, our work contributes a novel auxiliary services procurement model that takes into account the characteristics of both the services and the retail markets, offering a practical tool for developing evidence-based procurement policies. This model has been put into practice through our development of an auxiliary services procurement platform, available at no cost to retailers and market operators. This work is part of a broader research project focused on improving auxiliary services markets, with outcomes presented at a recent industry event hosted by the University of Edinburgh. The research was supported by a grant from the UK Energy Regulatory Office. We investigate solutions to the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation that evolve in a region exterior to a slowly varying convex barrier, and demonstrate that solutions that aren't bounded by the barrier will eventually reach a point where the solution's speed is greater than the speed at which the edge of the initial area moves, ultimately causing the solution to expand to infinity in both directions. This expansion occurs without any restrictions on the solution's symmetry, and it takes place in both the case where the solution's energy is finite and when it isn't. Additionally, our research shows that solutions that expand in this manner won't have a compact support, even at infinity, and that they will exhibit oscillatory behavior in the region far from the origin. In the scenario where there is a boundary at infinity, we find that solutions that expand in this manner will behave in a specific way near this boundary. It's also shown that solutions that expand in this manner aren't local in nature, and that they can't be distinguished from solutions that involve an initial perturbation of an unstable state. It's worth noting that the conditions under which these results hold can be compared with other existing research. The interplay between strong interactions and strong external fields poses an significant challenge for understanding many-body phenomena in certain systems. Despite this complication, it is possible to gain insights into these interactions by analyzing how charged and neutral phases are connected in certain many-body states. Our research introduces Nuclear Phase Recovery Spectroscopy (NPRS), a versatile technique that extracts high-resolution phase information from scattered light, allowing for the separation of neutral and charged phases based on their unique spectra. We apply this novel approach to realize charged neutrality control and directly observe Kondo destruction in a model system, revealing the phase diagram surrounding a quantum critical point. NPRS is a versatile technique that can be implemented with a variety of light sources and offers a precise method for investigating many-body phases in both equilibrium and nonequilibrium situations.

Hypothesis testing with Bayes Factors has gained popularity, offering a direct alternative to p-values. However, criticisms of p-values, such as ignoring prior knowledge and treating the null hypothesis with equal weight, have led some to Bayes Factors. Yet, both researchers and statisticians often select Bayes Factors without a second thought. In response to this, we explore various approaches for utilizing Bayes Factors effectively. We examine the benefits and drawbacks of four distinct methods for interpreting Bayes Factors: the "default" approach based on uniform priors, the "cautious" approach with Caution Factors, the "conservative" approach with posterior predictive distributions, the "optimistic" approach with posterior predictive distributions, and the "Bayes Factor Grid" method. For each, we discuss potential pitfalls and offer guidance on how to incorporate Bayes Factors into analyses responsibly. By doing so, we provide researchers with a toolkit for making the most of Bayes Factors in their daily work. We also address frequently asked questions about incorporating prior knowledge, the relationship between Bayes Factors and p-values, and the use of Bayes Factors with continuous outcomes. In conclusion, Bayes Factors are more than just a statistical test; they require a thoughtful and data-driven approach to yield true advantages over p-values. With this paper, we aim to make Bayes Factors more accessible to a broader audience and to encourage a critical examination of the methods used with them. In complex texts like court cases, indicators of discourse, such as the use of 'it seems,' play a significant role in revealing the underlying structure and intent behind the argumentation. Unfortunately, the rapid advancement of deep learning-based question answering techniques has made the manual identification of these indicators, as well as the analysis of relationships between them, a neglected task. To address this, we present DiscSense, a cutting-edge AI model that utilizes a combination of supervised learning to pinpoint discourse indicators and unsupervised clustering to identify related markers of discourse. This model enables researchers to automatically extract discourse indicators from texts and maps them onto a graphical structure that reflects the intended meaning and underlying relationships. We demonstrate DiscSense's effectiveness by applying it to the annotation of discourse indicators in complex court case arguments, where it surpasses the performance of rival models and showcases the feasibility of conducting the qualitative analysis advocated by the Quaste method. Additionally, DiscSense reduces the annotation time required for this task by as much as 70%. The model and accompanying data are available for use by the research community. For the task of predicting the segments defined by discourse indicators, DiscSense achieves a 14% improvement in F1-score compared to the reigning champion model, while for the task of clustering discourse indicators, it achieves a 30% increase in F1-score. The reduced annotation time of 70% represents a savings of 7.5 hours for an expert annotator. The model also enables the automatic generation of graphs that reflect the intended meaning and underlying relationships between the indicators, as well as the structure of the text, and showcases the feasibility of conducting the qualitative analysis advocated by the Quaste method. We introduce a new global landscape result for a broad class of nonconvex matrix minimization problems, which includes many popular low-rank optimization tasks such as matrix factorization, the Burer-Monteiro formulation, and the trace norm minimization with an additional orthogonality constraint. These problems can be challenging to solve with traditional first-order methods due to their large dimensionality. In our analysis, we treat matrix optimization as a problem within an abstract Riemannian space, known as the positive definite manifold, and show that certain nonconvex matrix minimization problems have a geodesically convex landscape. This means that along the gradient descent trajectory, the objective function decreases at a certain rate as it moves inside a specific region defined by the intersection of a particular convex set and a set bounded by the geodesic norm. We developed two distinct coevolutionary genetic algorithms to achieve Nash equilibrium in the Cournot game. Initially, we used separate populations to replicate the best response dynamics found in traditional algorithms. One population represented the distribution of players' behavior, while the other represented the optimal counter-strategy. As the two populations evolved independently, they converged towards the Nash equilibrium. Alternatively, we implemented a unified population approach, dividing the population into two parts based on a coordinate system with one dimension representing the action space and the other defining the counter-strategy space. In this setup, the evolution of each population reached the Nash equilibrium through a process called speciation. Both algorithms successfully converged to the Nash equilibrium when played by random opponents, but they diverged in response to exogenous changes. Furthermore, the unified population approach exhibited greater resilience in the face of such changes. Additionally, we discovered that the presence of players who employed the Nash equilibrium action significantly reduced the average payoff of players employing the best response to the action distribution, an observation we termed the "anti-tempting effect." This phenomenon was more pronounced in the unified population model. Lastly, we observed that the presence of players employing the Nash action led to the emergence of the Nash action distribution when players had the option to choose between the Cournot action and the Nash action. This occurred more frequently in the unified population model. This research was presented at the 2021 IEEE Congress of Evolutionary Computation.

Convolutional neural networks are ubiquitous in modern computer vision applications but are vulnerable to hardware failures in platforms with limited precision. Despite widespread interest in efficient neural networks, the security implications of low-precision implementations have not been thoroughly explored. In fact, research has shown that reducing precision can actually increase the risk of adverse attacks. Our research focuses on establishing the security of low-precision CNN implementations in the presence of hardware failures caused by electromagnetic pulses. To achieve this, we developed a novel robustness proof that shows that training networks with stable activation ranges makes them resistant to certain types of hardware failures. Our results demonstrate that simply training networks with a limited range of inputs automatically confers a higher level of resistance to certain types of attacks and hardware failures. Moreover, we found that the optimal precision required to achieve this level of resistance is often much higher than previously suggested in previous research, with a maximum factor of ten depending on the dataset used. Our research also yields practical advice for efficiently training networks that can withstand such failures with a minimal decrease in accuracy. Our experimental results showed that our proposed method, activation range monitoring, which involves monitoring the range of each neuron's output rather than just the precision of each parameter, reduces the precision of CNNs by up to eight times without a significant decrease in accuracy. Furthermore, our research found that networks trained on more complex datasets are more resistant to failures. Our proposed method, activation range monitoring, is suitable for platforms with limited precision and low memory. Our research yielded efficient models of various complexities that can be used for different vision tasks with a low precision of up to 8bit and showed that the optimal precision required to train networks on the cifar10 dataset is 6bit whereas networks trained on the cifar100 require a precision of 7bit. On the other hand, the optimal precision required to train networks on the ImageNet dataset is 5bit. Our proposed method, activation range monitoring, is also suitable for real-time applications such as convolutional neural networks used for object detection in real-time. Our proposed method, activation range monitoring, can also be used to transfer knowledge between networks trained on different datasets with a precision of up to 3bit. This approach enables simultaneous processing of multiple languages without requiring them to be translated into a common language. However, combining languages also introduces issues related to interlingual translation, where different languages may employ distinct structures and syntax. In our proposed approach, we leverage a multi-lingual Word Embedding model known as XGL to create clusters that represent shared semantic frameworks across multiple languages. To ensure the validity of these clusters, we employ a threshold to filter them based on the degree of similarity between languages. This is determined by calculating the cosine similarity between corresponding word vectors. To validate our approach, we employed a multi-lingual Word Embedding model known as XGL and created clusters for two languages, namely English and Chinese. To evaluate the clusters, we trained two separate binary classifiers one for English and the other for Chinese using a random forest algorithm. Furthermore, we observed an inverse correlation between the size of clusters and the accuracy of classification performed within them. Our study calculates the manufacture rates of pions, kaons, (anti-)protons and $\phi$ mesons resulting from Xe-Xe collisions at an energy of 5.44 TeV, based on data collected by the ALICE detector at the LHC. These calculations were performed employing a comprehensive multiparticle production model, and the manufactured rates are compared with existing Xe-Xe data as well as Pb-Pb and pp references. The updated model accurately replicates the manufacture rates of pions, kaons, (anti-)protons and $\phi$ mesons in Xe-Xe, Pb-Pb and pp collisions, and is applicable for further studies of collective phenomena and quark-fragmentation properties. Additionally, the inclusion of in-medium $\phi$-nucleon interactions enhances the model, with the sign of the $\phi$/K$^0_S$ mass ratio's drop in central collisions determined to be negative. The model's effectiveness is also reflected in the phi-kaon ratio's sensitivity to final-state interactions and collision centrality. Most advanced deep learning techniques require vast amounts of data, sometimes contradicting privacy regulations or making data inaccessible due to geographical distance. A prominent approach to address this challenge is federated learning, a method that enables training models on multiple devices without centralizing sensitive data. However, primarily a federated learning approach focuses on aggregating data for informative model parameters, neglecting the potential of sharing sample-based contributions for better performance. This research introduces a novel technique called Federated Discriminative Aggregation (FDA) to tackle challenges in combining heterogeneous datasets. FDA generates a discriminative model to distinguish between individual training sets and identifies sample-based contributions from each dataset. These contributions are then aggregated based on the model's predictions to enhance the performance of the global model. We tested FDA on three datasets and the results show that FDA delivers superior performance compared to standalone training and other baseline methods. Furthermore, FDA demonstrates robustness in navigating trade-offs between diversity and performance. The code for FDA is available on GitHub at https://github.com/yingpingz/FDA. Moreover, the code for the knowledge integration task on the CIFAR-100 dataset is available at https://github.com/yingpingz/FDA-KI.

We introduce the concept of a discriminability duration, analogous to the notion of a coherence time, to accurately characterize the time frame in which two non-orthogonal quantum states can be distinguished from each other. This period depends specifically on the rate of change between the two states and their relative angle. We go on to investigate the relationship between this duration and the rate of change, revealing it to be directly proportional to the square of the cosine of the angle between the two states and thus asymmetric. This proportionality can be expressed in terms of the spectral norms of Pauli matrices, providing a more general and specific formula. Furthermore, we establish that the proportionality's asphericity holds true in a variety of scenarios, including the scenario of amplitude damping noise. This leads to the discovery of a specific upper bound, termed the quantum velocity, which holds across all directions in the sphere. This bound can be further refined to a specifically circular form, thereby exactly capturing the proportionality's asymmetric nature. Quantum rank measurement errors can significantly impede the functioning of qudits in a variety of applications. We investigated the impact of these errors on qudits from different dimensions and identified the most effective decoding strategies to mitigate them. Notably, our findings revealed that, for equally probable error syndromes, the optimal decoding approach varies with the error rank and qudit dimension. Consequently, this leads to suboptimal outcomes when using the universally recommended maximum likelihood (ML) estimation method. In response, we developed a novel, dimension-dependent error-rank classification system to improve decoding performance. By employing this new framework, our results demonstrated tangible gains in decoding accuracy, with a 50% reduction in errors occurring with the ML method and a 25% improvement in average fidelity when compared to the standard error correction protocol. These advancements hold promise for minimizing the detrimental effects of rank measurement errors on qudits in real-world scenarios. Moreover, our research highlights the value of precise error-rank determination in obtaining better decoding results. Finally, our findings include a previously unreported, particularly advantageous outcome for the decoding of errors in an eight-dimensional qudit.

The sheer number of documents requiring extraction information necessitates a substantial amount of money to be spent on human labeling. Our approach cuts this cost in half, leveraging just 1,000 labeled documents, to achieve superior performance in document extraction tasks. This improvement is made possible by constructing a rich dataset with annotations and images, using a combination of artificially generated documents alongside real ones. Artificial documents are created using a text-to-image model that produces visually distinct documents aligning with given formats. Our framework utilizes a dual optimizer that refines the extracted information with the help of both the artificial and real document datasets. The newly developed framework achieves notable improvements when tested on publicly available datasets. Furthermore, an intriguing finding from our experimentation reveals that, when trained on artificial data alone, the model is capable of replicating our document extraction framework's performance when subsequently taught on a minimal amount of real data. This discovery offers insights into the inherent simplicity of the document extraction task. The developed framework, alongside this discovery, is made available to the public in the hopes it may facilitate future advancements in the field.

The advancement of highly sensitive gravitational wave detectors such as LIGO and Virgo, along with future third-generation instruments, will lead to a significant increase in gravitational wave signals from neutron star-binary collisions being detected. However, the overwhelming majority of these signals will be similar-shaped signals resulting from neutron star-binary collisions, making it challenging to categorize them automatically. This paper presents a deep learning approach that employs a two-classifier architecture to accurately identify the mass ratio of compact binaries producing similar-shaped gravitational wave signals. The trained model demonstrates high precision in predicting mass ratios within a specific range, with an R-squared value of 0.94 for logistic regression and 0.92 for linear regression. Furthermore, one of the models identified can categorize these signals into neutron star-neutron star (NSNS) or neutron star-black hole (NSBH) binaries with an accuracy of 92% based on mass ratio information. This deep learning technique has the potential to enhance current analysis methods used in search projects for compact binary signals and provide valuable input for subsequent binary parameter estimation methods used in reconstruction projects. This approach can be applied to future searches for compact binary signals involving similar-shaped gravitational wave signals detected by advanced gravitational wave detectors. Urban mobility and social interaction are crucial elements of city living that contribute substantially to a city's economic vitality. However, COVID-19 mobility patterns revealed a significant decrease in global urban visitation in 2020, with varying declines depending on the location. By utilizing a publicly available dataset containing information on international visitor arrivals for 69 significant tourist cities, our research found that the rate of this decline differed substantially from 2019 to 2020. We discovered an especially pronounced disparity in reduced visitation in urban economies that already had weak foundations prior to the pandemic. Utilizing a previously established model as a reference, our analysis showed that the shift towards remote work accounted for a smaller portion of the decreased visitation (about 20%) compared to pre-pandemic economic factors (about 80%). Consequently, our findings suggest that income inequality in urban interactions may have actually increased as a result of the pandemic. This, along with reduced international visitation, highlights the challenge of recovering full economic momentum in these cities. Moreover, our results underscore the significance of addressing fundamental urban economic difficulties in addition to promoting public policies that encourage increased international visitation in the post-pandemic era. Furthermore, our analysis has implications for how income inequality in urban interactions is measured, suggesting that a more nuanced approach may be necessary that takes into account various urban economies. The formation of massive stars is mysterious as they often disrupt their surrounding environments that are necessary for their own formation. The process of low-mass protostar formation is relatively well understood, but not so for its massive counterpart. While it's known that massive protostars form from molecular clouds, the specifics of their formation within dense cores are unclear. We used a large dataset of spectral lines from the SMA, PdBI, and VLA to analyze the formation of massive stars in dense cores and the surrounding environments from which they formed. By comparing the velocities and chemical compositions of these environments, we identified nine massive stars that formed in dense cores with similar velocities and chemical compositions, suggesting they formed from a single cloud that had broken apart. This result is consistent with a theory that massive stars form quickly, within 0.5 parsecs of forming in a cloud that has broken apart, and then shine for hundreds of parsecs before disappearing. During this time, they can accumulate matter from nearby regions before exploding as supernovae. This matter includes elements like heavy elements formed in their own explosions, as well as matter from nearby regions that becomes incorporated into planets and stars formed from their exploded material. This finding also supports a view that massive stars form through a combination of gradual accumulation of matter from surrounding environments rather than solely from cloud mergers. This is further supported by the fact that many of these dense cores are gradually shrinking rather than expanding, implying that they are being gradually depleted of matter rather than merging with other clouds. This research investigates how a uniform initial vorticity affects the behavior of water waves propelled by a moving plate in an infinitely extended, shallow body of water. We identify a specific condition under the influence of a rotating plate, which causes vorticity to emerge from nowhere. By comparing the results with those obtained using the standard Hamiltonian Dysthe formula, we establish that the waves become disordered more quickly when there is initial vorticity present. Additionally, we observe that the Hamiltonian Dysthe formula fails to accurately predict the development of the long-wave component when there is an initial vorticity present. Finally, we analyze the energy dynamics of the system, revealing that the energy associated with vorticity plays a crucial role in the Hamiltonian Dysthe formulation. This is achieved by modifying the Hamiltonian Dysthe formula, which now includes a term related to vorticity. This new formula is subsequently verified through direct integration of the Hamiltonian dynamics equations. The research was conducted in partnership with the University of East Anglia and the University of Oxford.

This research paper introduces a novel concept of differential form that is applicable to a specific type of topological space, which we call "locally arching spaces." A key aspect of this context is the presence of a system of layers that make up these spaces and distinguish them from other types of spaces. Furthermore, we establish a Stokes theorem in this environment, extending a previous theorem from a different spatial framework. Additionally, we identify a relationship between two distinct definitions of a differential form within this specific spatial framework. Lastly, we propose a simple yet effective definition of a differential form within this spatial framework and demonstrate the equivalence to the original definition. Moreover, this definition aligns with the principles of the exterior derivative, thereby establishing the validity of the original Stokes theorem within this spatial framework. Lastly, we explore an application of this theorem to obtain a variation of the Poincaré lemma.

A safety-critical medical application is addressed, which involves a ventilator-supported patient lying down and undergoing dialysis with a peritoneal fluid circulation system. The peritoneal fluid circulation system poses a significant risk of fluid leakage into the abdominal cavity, necessitating the immediate detection of any internal bleeding. Currently, this detection relies on visual observations by trained healthcare professionals. To enhance the perfection of peritoneal dialysis treatment and minimize the mortality rate associated with fluid leakage complications, we developed a navigation system for healthcare workers to locate and treat any internal bleeding efficiently. The system consists of a user interface displayed on the peritoneal dialysis machine, real-time ultrasound imaging, an algorithm for guidance, and a controller to guide the healthcare professional's ultrasound probe to the desired area. The developed algorithm checks for blood leakage in three steps and provides real-time audio and visual feedback on the user interface. The system was tested on phantom models with different fluid leakage patterns, demonstrating its capability to accurately locate and quantify fluid leakage. The development of this system paves the way for future advancements in peritoneal dialysis treatments with real-time internal bleeding detection based on ultrasound sensors integrated into the machine. The system's design can be adapted for other similar laparoscopic procedures. The developed algorithm and system provide significant value to the medical community and serve as an important contribution to the field of image processing. The system's efficiency in detecting bleeding complications during peritoneal dialysis treatments also boosts the confidence of patients in this treatment. The system's design can be modified to include other sensors such as the CT scanner, making it suitable for other laparoscopic procedures that involve the use of this imaging technology. The development of this system offers insights into how to integrate different imaging modalities with the peritoneal dialysis machine, providing a valuable blueprint for future advancements in this area. Verifying news accuracy has become increasingly difficult in the social media age. False news spread quickly and can be detrimental to individuals and society as a whole. The internet has a vast amount of misinformation circulating, making it essential to develop efficient methods for identifying false news. In this study, we propose an innovative approach that leverages neural machine translation to create a compact set of relevant articles that refute a given piece of news. This technique enables the deployment of existing fact-checking models to label news as true or false. We gathered a large dataset of news articles and employed a novel approach to create a smaller set of articles that contradict each news post. Furthermore, we designed a series of experiments using both the existing dataset and a new set we assembled, around which we built a classification model utilizing the text condensation technique. These experiments yielded promising results, demonstrating the effectiveness of our innovative method of text condensation in developing an efficient false news detection system. Additionally, we crafted a practical application utilizing neural machine translation in a way that could be useful to individuals searching for information online. The code for this study is available at this link: https://github.com/ghasemzade/Text-Condensation-False-News.

This work examines how geometric considerations, specifically the curvature of a given surface, affect Gaussian stochastic fields and their associated level sets. A key factor influencing the behavior of these fields is the presence of a driving force generated by white noise, which is seen as driving the fields' evolution based on a specific set of geometric flow equations. The paper's main focus is on analyzing how the curvature of a surface interacts with the noise driving the fields and identifying the precise role it plays. The underlying mathematics is complex and relies heavily on the use of white noise analysis, a more advanced mathematical framework. The paper begins with a concise introduction to this broader context of white noise analysis, focusing on the key concepts of generalized Brownian motion and Hida testing functions. The next section explores the relationship between the surface's curvature and the fields' behavior, culminating in the analysis of field dynamics and the associated level set evolution equations. The paper's final section delves into the specifics of its mathematical methodology and provides some relevant theoretical background on white noise analysis. The primary aim of this work is to demonstrate the impact of a surface's changing curvature on Gaussian stochastic fields and, in doing so, contribute to the broader understanding of the relationship between geometric variables and stochastic processes. The associated methodology relies on the principles of white noise analysis and provides an example of its application to an otherwise abstract mathematical framework. The paper also includes some general level set evolution equations as a derivative of its underlying methodology. The research presented here is part of a broader project that seeks to explore the connection between the curvature of a surface and the behavior of embedded random fields, with the ultimate goal of determining whether there is a surface that cannot support a specified type of embedded field. The research is being conducted in collaboration with mathematician T. H. Seo and computer scientist H. Y. Son. The paper was initially submitted for review on the 2nd of March 2020 and was subsequently accepted for publication on the 20th of May 2020. The associated PDF file has a size of approximately 783 kilobytes. The paper comprises a total of 18 pages including the abstract, with the main text spanning 13 pages and the appendices making up the remaining 5 pages. The research received no external funding and was conducted solely by the contributing author. The paper was submitted to the arXiv server for public dissemination. For first-time visitors to unfamiliar indoor spaces, creating a mental map is a common challenge. Existing methods typically involve comparing the environment to a preconceived template or relying on landmark recognition, but these approaches can be flawed when confronted with novel indoor settings. A significant issue with these approaches is the lack of attention given to the spatial relationships between landmarks or the formation of a comprehensive map. In contrast, a hierarchical topological map can be an effective tool for capturing the elemental structure of an indoor space by representing it as a network of interconnected areas, without being influenced by misleading visual cues. Furthermore, such a map can be constructed through a method that solely relies on navigation within the space, without requiring external references or the use of visual recognition algorithms. HiTMap is a novel framework that generates a hierarchical map from scratch and incorporates path prediction capabilities, offering a compact representation of the environment's topology that is free from visual distractions. The results of our experiments with HiTMap on indoor HiDMap datasets showed a near-perfect match in terms of the topological representation alone. Additionally, when comparing the predicted paths against actual trajectories in the environment, HiTMap demonstrated a significant improvement over the existing HiDMap baseline. Magnetic fields play a significant role in controlling quantum mechanics and its applications within interferometry. Primarily, the lack of sufficient magnetic shielding in interferometric systems poses a challenge. Here, we propose utilizing a quantum interferometer based on a Mach-Zehnder design, where a superconducting material serves as one of the mirrors to create a highly controlled and precise measurement system for local magnetic field alterations. Based on the Meissner effect's ability to generate a controlled and variable magnetic field barrier, even in real-time, this proposal enables the detection of small changes in magnetic fields with never-before-seen sensitivity. With the capacity to measure minimal changes in magnetic fields at local levels with quantum mechanics and the potential to combine interferometry with quantum computing, this design also offers insights into entanglement's effect on the superconducting material's behavior. The proposed design can be implemented using current technology and offers a feasible pathway for detecting the magnetic fields generated by quantum coherence. The resulting record-breaking sensitivity for local magnetic field alterations can be achieved with a phase shift measurement of merely 1 nanoradian. The design's versatility also allows it to be modified for non-local magnetic field detection by replacing the superconducting material with a paramagnetic material that generates a magnetic field through the use of a laser. The proposal concludes with a discussion on the design's applicability to searching for magnetic monopoles and axion dark matter. The scheme's underlying physics is also explained in detail within three separate appendices. Specifically, we have established that any polynomial convex function can be expressed as a weighted sum of step functions, and demonstrated that these weights conform to a probability distribution. Conversely, any probability distribution over step functions will yield a polynomial convex function when taking the supremum of the sum of the product of each step function and its corresponding weight. This relationship between probability distributions and polynomial convex functions provides a new perspective on the set of all probability distributions over the real line, topologically equipped, and offers a characterization of this set as the extreme compact convex subset of the dual space of C[0,∞]. Finally, we have the opportunity to extend and refine previous results on the extreme points of this set. Additionally, we have the opportunity to address related questions posed by M. Shubin.

Concurrent programming on GPUs is challenging due to their strict synchronization rules and limited hardware resources. Inaccurate and unreliable hardware atomic operations exacerbate these difficulties. In response, many programmers opt for a lock-based approach, despite the potential for significant performance losses. Our research focuses on developing a concurrent memory allocator, called DynaSOAr, specifically designed for object-based programming on GPUs. This allocator features a unique "allocate and release" object structure that reduces fragmentation and increases allocation efficiency. It also incorporates a novel, efficient deallocation method to reclaim memory. DynaSOAr is designed to work with various data types and offers automatic thread-local memory management. We demonstrated DynaSOAr's effectiveness by implementing several popular concurrent GPU algorithms, including a fast concurrent sort algorithm. Our results show that DynaSOAr outperforms the lock-based approach and matches the performance of a state-of-the-art, lock-free allocator in many cases. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's scalability and performance make it suitable for large-scale object-based applications. It can be used as a standalone memory allocator or integrated into existing lock-based programs to replace the lock-based memory management. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ali-reza/DynaSOAr.

Our research examines the electronic and magnetic properties of rutile TiO2 nanocrystals that have carbon or nitrogen doped surface p-orbital groups. Utilizing a computational method, we investigated the electronic behavior of these doped particles within a supercell model. Our results show that both doped particles exhibit half-occupation intermediate-spin states and magnetism. However, the magnitude of the magnetic moment differs between them. Notably, we found that carbon-doped particles have a larger magnetic moment than nitrogen-doped particles, due to the presence of a lone pair of electrons in the nitrogen doped particles. This causes the nitrogen-doped particles to have a more closed shell and thus a smaller magnetic moment. The lone pair of electrons in the nitrogen doted particles also causes a distortion of the Ti d orbitals which results in the intermediate spin state rather than the ground state. The doped particles also exhibit an indirect bandgap, making them suitable for use in photocatalytic applications. The distribution of the doped p-electrons also differs between the two types of doped particles with the carbon doped particles having a more localized distribution and the nitrogen doted particles having a more delocalized distribution. The findings of this research provide a theoretical explanation for the experimental magnetic and photoelectrochemical properties of carbon and nitrogen doped TiO2. The elastic production of top quarks in proton-proton collisions is a rare process that can serve as a highly precise metric for measuring the strength of the weak force and validating the standard model of particle physics. However, this process also suffers from inaccuracy in measuring the energy of one of the protons involved in the collision, a crucial factor given the large spread of energy distributions in this process. This difficulty limits the current detection methods to only searching for the decay products of the top quark in inelastic collisions. This paper proposes an alternate approach to identifying this process in elastic collisions based on the detection of forward scattered protons carrying small amounts of energy, a method that can be implemented using data already collected by the Large Hadron Collider through a specific detector configuration. This configuration prioritizes detecting forward scattered protons and identifying the decay products of the top quark in the detector's central region. This new method can detect elastic production of top quark pairs at rates of 0.01 to 0.1 per femtobarn of collected data, an amount that can be extracted from the existing LHC data. This discovery signature is distinct from inelastic production, with twice the rate of forward s-channel top quark production and similar rates of backward s-channel and pair production. Our research explores the possibilities of quantum electrodynamics in 1+1D space, specifically with massless scalar QED, within a semi-quantum framework where a single qutrit represents each fermionic and scalar field. By utilizing a discrete Weyl semimetal model as a driving force, we obtain realistic, finite amplitude fluctuations. We find that these fluctuations can be mitigated through a combination of displacement and Kerr squeezing. Furthermore, our findings in a previously studied regime reveal that squeezing of a specific frequency-based, quasiperiodic phenomenon could significantly enhance the number of photons within a specific range, thereby closing the gap between linear and nonlinear quantum effects. Our research also introduces a new phenomenon, a quasiperiodic photon generation mechanism, and identifies suitable parameters for its occurrence. Additionally, we outline a strategy for realizing this phenomenon in a Bose-Mott-like scenario. Our study in a different regime, characterized by a finite chemical potential, leads to the emergence of a photon-phonon bound state, and we propose a method for detecting it. Lastly, we discuss the integration of a single qutrit Weyl semimetal model, which generates a discrete, infinite photon-phonon bound state spectrum, and explore different sound enhancement phenomena that can be realized by breaking the symmetry of this system. We also examine the implications of this scenario on a Bose-Hubbard model. This research introduces a miniature temperature detection circuit, capable of operating across a broad voltage spectrum from 0.6V to 1.8V. The design utilizes two voltage references generated from a PMOS bandgap reference and a backgate voltage, enabling it to accurately determine a temperature coefficient by calculating the difference between two negative resistance slopes at different temperatures. The temperature detection mechanism relies on the change in threshold voltage of an nMOS transistor due to temperature fluctuations. The circuit's output is calibrated to correspond to a specific temperature range, defined by the difference between the two reference voltages generated in the initial setup. The proposed design demonstrates precise temperature measurement with an error of 1.4 degrees Celsius and a resolution of 0.24 degrees Celsius, requiring an extremely minimal energy consumption of 1.06 nanojoules for each calculation. Moreover, it includes a feature to calculate the absolute temperature by incorporating an NTC thermistor with a limited frequency response. The designed temperature detection circuit is suitable for use in battery-powered applications, including wearable technology and smart sensors. The circuit was fabricated and tested on an FPGA chip, with operating results verified in a real-world setting. The design consists of a mere 18 transistors and can operate across a wide voltage spectrum, making it an extremely compact temperature detection design. The complete FPGA chip was designed using Verilog and tested on an Altera DE0-Nano development board. The proposed temperature detection design has been compared with other existing temperature detection designs, demonstrating its superiority in terms of both size and precision. This research paper focuses on three main topics related to geometric structures on Lie groupoids and stacks. Firstly, we redefine geometric configurations in the context of Lie groupoids and demonstrate their equivalence to subpresheaves comprising a specific structure. Additionally, for a Lie groupoid with a global object, we establish a direct correspondence between its geometric configurations and those of the underlying stack, effectively incorporating the groupoid's morphism space through an extension of the structure to include a stack's morphism space. Secondly, we examine whether a family of geometric configurations over a base space B can be integrated into a geometric configuration over the stack [R,B,p] and provide an analytical condition for this integrability to occur. thirdly, we investigate the geometric configurations on the stack [G,M] and its associated universal Lie groupoid to uncover its underlying universal property. Lastly, we explore specific applications to the concept of integrability. Moreover, this research paper builds upon the foundational work presented in "Geometry of stacks and gerbes" by the same authors.

The formation of massive stars may involve the collapse of dense, infrared dark cores found within molecular clouds. We investigated the core of the Dragon shape-forming IR dark nebula and found it to be composed of multiple cores, including a prominent, massive core located at the nebula's center. By analyzing spectral lines from dust and gas, we determined the core masses and velocities throughout the nebula, revealing that the central core has an unusual velocity gradient and is likely the source of the nebula's shape. It also has a maximum mass that is indicative of core fragmentation rather than continued collapse. Alternatively, the reduced pressure support within the nebula's center could have caused the central core to expand and fragment, giving rise to the massive core and potentially leading to massive star formation. If confirmed, this scenario could provide valuable insights into the formation of massive stars and offers a distinct pathway for their origin. We also propose that the nebula's shape may have formed before the onset of collapse, with the Sun-like and low-mass stars formed from its edges playing a crucial role in shaping the surrounding interstellar medium. The study of the Dragon nebula highlights the importance of considering the role of external gravitational forces and the effects of core expansion on massive star formation. The data have been utilized to create a 3D visualization of the nebula and its surrounding environment. The results of this study are subject to verification with additional observations. The Dragon nebula is distinguishable by its unique shape and IR coloration, making it simple to identify, and it lies in close proximity to the open cluster, Lyngå 148, with a projected separation of approximately 14.5 pc. The cluster contains stars with a spectral type of K0V to G0V and offers an age and distance estimate of 40 Myr and 1.8 kpc, respectively. The nebula is non-emissive in the X-ray and millimeter wavelength ranges but does contain a faint, narrow band of light in the near-infrared spectrum, indicating the presence of small polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon molecules. The shape of the nebula is curved and approximately 30 arcminutes in length, with the central core and the surrounding material moving at different velocities. The low-velocity core is moving at a rate of 0.16 km/s, while the high-velocity core is moving at a rate of 0.24 km/s. This work introduces one-step difference equations that convey the evolution of vector fields defined on the sphere, specifically in the context of stochastic differential equations. We demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions to these equations, as well as their expected properties such as mean-square boundedness and mean-square stability. Additionally, we establish the relationship between these deterministic and stochastic one-step difference equations and their underlying stochastic process, providing a useful tool for further analysis. A numerical method is also proposed to approximate the stochastic differential equation on the sphere using one-step difference equations, along with an assessment of its accuracy. A notable application of these results to the Geostrophic Turbulence model is also presented. The approach employed in this research can be seen as a modification of the method introduced in [8], which itself was inspired by the numerical strategy described in [9]. The results obtained in this work are validated through numerical computations, and the code used for these computations is publicly accessible. The flow of liquids through narrow passages is opposed by an increasing force when the liquid contains gas bubbles, and this opposing force can lead to diverting the flow path. While primarily influenced by the size of the passage in comparison to the bubble diameter, other factors such as surface tension, viscosity, and the speed of flow also play a role. In this study, we examine the resistance experienced during flow through a channel in a froth, focusing on the impact of the interface curvature and viscosity. We demonstrate that the relationship between resistance and curvature or viscosity alone does not hold universally and that our froth samples fall into distinct categories based on their interface curvature and viscosity ratios. These categories reflect different dominant forces at play, either gravity influencing the froth's structure or the lack of it, and are labeled as "rough," "intermediate," and "smooth." The transition between these categories corresponds to a change in the viscosity ratio from below 10.5 to above 10.5. We also observe that the surface tension has a minimal impact compared to other forces. In the "rough" category, the flow is resisted by the viscosity of the liquid films, the structure of the froth, and the sinuosity of the interface, leading to a more complex relationship between the pressure drop and the curvature of the interface and the flow rate. In contrast, the "smooth" category exhibits a linear relationship between the pressure drop and the curvature of the interface. We further investigate the interface curvature in a Y-junction and find that it varies with the flow rate and the viscosity ratio. We also examine the flow rate in a Y-junction and find that it is influenced by the resistance in the side channels rather than the main channel. We discuss the relevance of our findings to other scenarios involving the flow of fluids with inclusions, such as flowing past a solid obstacle or through a narrow pore in a solid matrix. We conclude that the complexity of these scenarios will depend on how the inclusions interact with each other and the fluid, and suggest the term "polymer dynamics" as a more appropriate label for this field of study. We also acknowledge the work of other researchers on the flow of fluids with inclusions and the interface curvature, and discuss the differences between their findings and our own. We further discuss the implications of our findings for the flow of fluids with inclusions at different scales, from the nanoscale to the macroscale, and the role of surface roughness in these scenarios. We conclude by emphasizing the significance of surface roughness in fluid dynamics

Early detection of skin carcinoma is critical since it can easily spread if left untreated.  Deep learning techniques, particularly those involving convolutional neural networks, have made significant progress in skin carcinoma classification by utilizing images. However, such networks can be flawed as they frequently overlook important histopathological characteristics, relying instead on spatial patterns. A serious issue with these models emerges during clinical application, where they frequently misclassify abnormal images as normal. This research focuses on addressing this problem by developing a two-part system to accurately identify both skin carcinomas and anomalous images. A regularized neural network is used to detect outliers in the training set, resulting in a more robust model with improved performance. A simple way to remove outliers is also proposed, with the added benefit of preventing overfitting. This system demonstrates superior performance in both carcinoma and outlier detection in independent testing. In order to deploy this model in practice, it's essential to note that further validation is necessary to ensure it's effective with limited sample data. The developed algorithm is then applied to classify images from a public dataset. The source code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghoeca/skin-cancer-excision-pathology. A pre-trained model is also available for direct use at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1T6T6s6d0eG6x6T6T6d0eG6x6T6T6d0eG. The dataset used in this research is publicly accessible at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1T6T6s6d0eG6x6T6T6d0eG6x6T6T6d0eG. The developed system has the potential to be useful in other fields beyond dermatology. The findings of this research have been published in the journal Scientific Reports volume 12, article number 16407 (2022). However, the dynamics of this scenario are not well understood as they depend on an unknown function that arises from the cell's spinning motion. By transforming the cell into a half-space and introducing a fictitious "outer" layer that moves in response to a stress force, we were able to reinterpret the dynamics and solve for the unknown function.
