We conducted a detailed analysis of the TMC-1 ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers, with the aim of pinpointing the frequency values of their rotational lines. Initially, researchers identified two ethynyl cyclopentadiene features in the TMC-1 spectrum, located at 6.029 and 6.081 GHz, which they attributed to the 8K-7K$_{1}$ (E) and 8K-7K$_{2}$ (E) rotational transitions of two different ethynyl cyclopentadiene molecules. However, due to the limited frequency resolution of their former receiver, the precise line shape remained unclear. Under the assumption that the ethynyl group frequency remains unchanged, we determined the cyclopentadiene frame frequencies for both isomers. Based on these values and a comparison with laboratory-generated ethynyl cyclopentadiene, we were able to accurately fit the line profiles and thus confidently detected the two isomers, denoted as c-C$_{5}$H$_{5}$C$\equiv$C at 6.029 GHz and with a cyclopentadiene frame frequency 48.9 MHz higher than the 1979 prediction, and also confirming the presence of the CN variant, c-C$\equiv$N-C$_{5}$H$_{5}$ at 6.081 GHz, 53.4 MHz greater than the 1979 calculated value. Additionally, we determined the beam-convolved line widths of both features, which amount to approximately 15.4 kHz. Given that ethynyl cyclopentadiene possesses a structure similar to benzene, we analyzed its rotational line widths in comparison to those of TMC-1 benzene, discovering that the line widths of both features are essentially identical, with a line width of 15.4 kHz for the 8K$_{s}$ J=7, K$_{s}$=4, 8K$_{c}$ J=7, K$_{c}$=3 doublet. Lastly, we updated the earlier calculations of ethynyl cyclopentadiene line frequencies based on a more precise determination of the dipole moment, leading to a frequency shift of 53.4 MHz compared to the 1979 prediction.

In neural machine translation, assigning focus to words within the source sentence has been a successful technique to improve targeted post-editing tasks by prioritizing crucial elements. However, when it comes to text generation tasks like abstract creation, the concept of focus remains under-explored. We propose the look-ahead focus model, which assigns a level of emphasis to words in the source sentence that will have the most impact on the target sentence, particularly useful for creating concise summaries. Unlike traditional focus models, our approach determines the degree of emphasis based on the target sentence's likelihood, thereby directly correlating with the importance of source words for the generated summary. We use the Cognitive Walkthrough method to validate our intuitive approach, showing that focusing on words with high prior probability is essential for reducing unnecessary information. Evaluations using the NIST and ROUGE metrics on the MEAD abstract creation dataset demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed model. Moreover, the model's ability to prioritize essential source words is reflected in lower cognitive load scores from our user study, further confirming the effectiveness of our approach. The code for the look-ahead focus model is available at this link https://github.com/ghulam-sabih/Neural-Machine-Interpretation.

The widespread adoption of grid computing technology outside of Europe and the United States faced significant challenges due to cultural, language, and technical barriers. A grid computing project based in Brazil, the SGI/GRID, successfully overcame these obstacles by employing a translational approach. This approach involved creating interfaces that bridged the gaps between different systems and allowed for seamless communication, thus facilitating the integration of diverse components into a unified framework. This paper examines the methodology and outcomes of this translational method in the context of the SGI/GRID. It also explores the implications for other grid computing projects operating in complex, multinational environments. The paper concludes by drawing on the experience of the SGI/GRID to provide guidance for future grid computing developments. The development of the grid computing framework in the paper serves as a specific example, and the underlying principles it employs are applicable to a broader range of complex systems. This model utilizes the fractal mass variation with scale to define the mass function of dark matter and incorporates a nonlinear equation to describe the evolution of the Hubble parameter. Both the mass function and the equation for the Hubble parameter are analytically solved in the model, which has an analytical expression for the deceleration-acceleration transition scale. This combined model provides a good fit to the observational data of the cosmic age, the current acceleration, and the fluctuation in the fractal scale. Furthermore, it predicts the fractal scale, the age of the universe, and the rate of change of the fractal scale with a high degree of accuracy. Additionally, the model includes a novel interpretation of the Hubble constant and the cosmological constant, which is compatible with the high-value lambda-CDM model. It also predicts that the cosmological constant and the Hubble constant are correlated with each other. This combined model offers an alternative to the standard model of the cosmos and provides testable predictions regarding the cosmological constant, the rate of change of the fractal scale, and the accuracy with which the cosmic microwave background fluctuations follow a fractal pattern. Our research provides a detailed breakdown of the J/ψ particle decaying into a photon and invisible matter, missing all but its electromagnetic radiation. We calculated the J/ψ scattering cross-section off protons using various quantum field theories that explain the nature of neutrinos and dark energy. Incorporating J/ψ production cross-section and branching ratio into the calculation, we determined the detection probability for J/ψ particles decaying into a photon and invisible matter. This detection probability was then added to the total number of J/ψ particles, allowing us to recover visible and invisible matter from J/ψ decays. This recovery process is relevant to deep inelastic scattering off J/ψ targets. Our study showed that in the standard model, the detection probability for J/ψ decaying into a photon and invisible matter is essentially 1, so it has no effect on scattering off J/ψ targets. In contrast, the detection probability is less than 1 for J/ψ decaying into a photon and invisible matter in the context of the left-handed left-handed light sterile neutrino and the scalar dark matter field theories. This result implies that J/ψ targets are more efficient for detecting light sterile neutrinos and scalar dark matter than deep inelastic scattering off proton targets. Specifically, we found that J/ψ targets can detect left-handed light sterile neutrinos with masses less than 7.60 GeV and scalar dark matter with masses less than 0.56 GeV, both with a significance of at least 5. With the J/ψ production rate at a few hundred GeV-s, we calculated the J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter as detectable at electron-positron colliders with a luminosity of at least 10^31 cm-2s-1, with the J/ψ moving vertically through the detector. This setup allows for the detection of light sterile neutrinos with masses less than 3.90 GeV and scalar dark matter with masses less than 0.39 GeV. With a J/ψ energy range of 20 to 65 GeV and assuming that J/ψ decays into a photon and invisible matter with 100% efficiency, we estimated the J/ψ production rate required to detect light sterile neutrinos with masses less than 3.77 GeV and scalar dark matter with masses less than 0.37 GeV at a significance of at least 5. This necessary J/ψ production rate ranges from 10^31 to 10^32 GeV/s

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across different dimensional domains, including scatters, tensors, and multivariate functions, and demonstrates the universality of the spectrum in each case. Unlike traditional singular spectrum analysis, which relies heavily on the autocorrelation matrix being well-conditioned, MFSSA instead focuses on the most significant singular components to determine the optimal lag matrix. This approach allows MFSSA to successfully decompose time series data even when the autocorrelation matrix exhibits severe ill-conditioning. Furthermore, MFSSA is invariant to the scaling of the variables, making it suitable for analyzing data across different dimensional domains. The application of MFSSA to mock and real-world datasets demonstrates its effectiveness, particularly in removing noise from multivariate functional time series. The R software code for implementing MFSSA is also provided. The approach presented in this study can be viewed as a generalization of the innovative singular spectrum analysis method introduced in Athankar et al. (2021). We investigate the long-term behavior of a stochastic process where a random walk continues as long as it remains within a specified boundary, and it halts once it crosses either boundary. We consider four distinct variants of this model, each defined by specific boundary conditions and with the random walk driven by either Brownian motion or a discrete time random walk. We examine the random process that represents the duration of the walk for each variant and show that its expectation eventually plateaus as the walk progresses, a phenomenon we call global persistence. We further find that the expected long-term duration of the walk can be substantial, increasing exponentially with its current depth when driven by a discrete time random walk, but only increasing logarithmically with its current depth when driven by a continuous time random walk driven by a Poisson process. We believe that our results, which include a number of sharp theorems and weaker intermediate results, provide valuable insights into the behavior of stochastic processes restricted to a given domain. We also discuss the relationship between these phenomena and more general models, offering potential applications to mathematical finance, genetics, and geology. We end by examining the predicted behavior of these models at their boundaries, finding that the random walk's distribution when it finally halts is asymptotically Gaussian when driven by a discrete time random walk but uniformly distributed when driven by a continuous time random walk driven by a Poisson process. We believe that these results, which may appear local in nature, are actually crucial components of our broader findings about global persistence. We acknowledge that our results extend previously known findings about discrete time random walks but drive a sharper analysis of continuous time random walks that relies on a new application of the large deviation principle. We also recognize that our research provides a novel interpretation of the boundaries in the context of continuous time random walks. Understanding the intricacies of nuclei in histopathology images is crucial for diagnosing and predicting cancer patient outcomes. Accurate identification of nuclei is essential for analyzing image features, but it's challenging due to overlapping cells, poor staining, and varying sizes. To address this, a network called W-Net was developed to specifically tackle nucleus segmentation within pancreatic cancer images. Composed of two consecutive convolutional neural networks, W-Net first learns to detect cell boundaries and then locate the centers of cells. Evaluating W-Net showed superior performance compared to competing approaches and current state-of-the-art models, with a 5.6% improvement in PANSTAINED score and a 7.1% decrease in Dice coefficient variance. Furthermore, W-Net effectively learned features at multiple cellular scales, enabling direct application to other cancer types with minimal modification. The open-source W-Net code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghruan/W-Net.

The accuracy of elastography, a technique that uses ultrasound to determine the mechanical properties of tissues, can be compromised when the distance between the elastography and ultrasound imaging arrays exceeds a certain limit. This limitation results from the side effects of elastography calculations, specifically the appearance of artifacts that falsely suggest tissue properties are different than they truly are, and the difficulty of obtaining clear images far from the source of the elastography. To overcome these challenges, a virtual origin method has been developed which allows for a more precise estimation of lateral shifts during elastography. This new approach uses the synthetic aperture capabilities of ultrasound technology to its advantage by selecting the optimal location for the virtual origin from which elastography calculations are begun. This virtual origin can be chosen from a range of locations, both near and far from the ultrasound imaging arrays, making it possible to obtain more accurate information about the mechanical properties of tissues located at greater distances from the elastography array. This virtual origin method works effectively in conjunction with other image processing techniques such as speckle reduction and blood vessel removal, and has been successfully tested on a range of phantom models and real-time elastography data. The resulting information about tissue mechanics obtained with this virtual origin method is significantly more reliable than other techniques available today. The virtual origin method can be implemented using a variety of ultrasound technologies including linear array, curvilinear array, and 3D matrix array ultrasound systems. The development of this method provides a foundation for even more advanced techniques such as real-time elastography and the determination of tissue mechanics in multiple dimensions. In emergency situations like natural disasters, searching for individuals who have gone missing requires finding areas where people may have been last seen. This process can be facilitated by identifying probable paths recent casualties may have taken. To this end, we are tasked with determining the most likely trajectories individuals may have followed in the aftermath of an earthquake. This problem is an instance of an inverse reconstruction challenge, where we have existing knowledge of how the earthquake's effects propagate and the movements of potential casualties, and we must recover the movements of the casualties. Unlike traditional reconstruction challenges, inverse reconstruction challenges do not fall under the category of optimization problems, but rather stem from a forward dynamics model. We can obtain the desired movements of the casualties by solving an optimization problem that minimizes the difference between their actual and predicted movements. However, having multiple possible trajectories that are equally likely could complicate the search effort. Therefore, we prioritize short trajectories over longer ones. We can formulate this as a non-convex optimization problem that involves a combination of a forward dynamics model and a neural network, and solve it using a regularized conditional GAN that generates plausible movements of the casualties. We evaluate our method on a simulated earthquake scenario and find that it compares favorably to other baselines. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method when compared to other movement prediction models, and show that it is capable of distinguishing between valid and fake trajectories. Furthermore, we analyze the problem and derive an upper bound on the expected mean squared error of the estimated trajectories. Finally, we apply our method to a real earthquake scenario and use the predicted trajectories to guide our search for missing individuals, and show that it is an efficient search strategy. We make our code available to the public.

Following this interaction path, a single Higgs doublet can give rise to the dark matter WIMP state and we have the option to choose either a "thick" or "thin" Higgs doublet to describe the dark sector. Within this framework, we have specific production and decay processes for Dark Matter and Higgs bosons. Consequently, our model yields two distinct cross-section versus mass profiles for the Dark Matter-Higgs boson interaction and we have identified three distinct mechanisms by which a Dark Matter particle could interact with Standard Model particles: via the easy implementation of 2-to-2 processes, via 2-to-3 processes that require additional particles, as well as 1-to-2 processes that involve the creation of a Higgs boson from the vacuum. Moreover, we have the capacity to control the Easy Penguin process's dominance over the EPEP process with the appropriate choice of mass parameter. Lastly, we have also explored the model's predictions for LHC through Deep Neural Network-based tools and our findings suggest that the most readily observable outcome at the LHC through Dark Sectors at 8 GeV would be the production of Dark Matter coupled to a Higgs boson, followed by the decay of this Dark Matter particle into two jets. Consequently, our analysis indicates that the Easy Scoto-Seesaw model can be distinguished from other "easy" scenarios via the detection of this particular outcome at the LHC through Dark Sectors at 8 GeV. Lastly, our findings are applicable to complex singlet Dark Matter scenarios.
